citations.quote: Let knots be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented S³ and let I=[0,1]. Let C_sm be their smooth concordance classes, where equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in S³×I. Let C_top be their locally flat topological concordance classes in that product. Let C_ex be their exotic-smooth concordance classes: equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W together with an orientation-preserving homeomorphism of pairs (W,∂W)≅(S³×I,S³×{0,1}) matching the endpoint knots. For a nonzero integer n set R_n=Z[1/|n|]. Let C^{1/n} be the classes under equivalence witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W with boundary the two standard endpoint 3-spheres such that each boundary inclusion induces an isomorphism H_i(S³;R_n)→H_i(W;R_n) for every i. A knot is pseudo-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth 4-manifold homeomorphic to B⁴, with the boundary identified with the standard S³. A knot is Z[1/|n|]-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth 4-manifold whose boundary inclusion is an isomorphism on homology with coefficients R_n. These are sets of equivalence classes; this definition alone asserts no group structure.

derivations.claim: Since W is contractible, its reduced integral homology vanishes; the boundary hypothesis gives ∂W≅S³. These facts establish the homological conditions in the statement but do not determine the smooth diffeomorphism type.
The implication W≅B⁴ is precisely the smooth complement assertion invoked in the CDR ordinary-smooth branch. It does not follow from contractibility by a handle cancellation argument supplied here.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice as required by the chosen tubular-neighborhood and peripheral-system data. Let K be a smooth oriented knot with compact exterior E_K, positive meridian mu_K, and preferred longitude lambda_K on the boundary torus. The zero-framed surgery manifold M(K) is the closed oriented 3-manifold obtained by gluing D²×S¹ to E_K so that the meridian boundary circle of D²×{1} is identified with lambda_K and the core {0}×S¹ is identified with mu_K. The orientation extends the orientation of E_K across the filling. Thus the filling slope is the preferred zero-linking longitude; the definition asserts no 4-manifold bounded by M(K).

Let $X$ be a four-dimensional manifold with boundary and let $W$ be a compact surface with boundary. An embedding $e:(W,\partial W)\to(X,\partial X)$ is proper when $e^{-1}(\partial X)=\partial W$. It is locally flat at an interior point of $W$ when there are neighborhoods of the point and its image and a homeomorphism of pairs from those neighborhoods to $(\mathbb R^4,\mathbb R^2)$, with the standard linear plane $\mathbb R^2\subset\mathbb R^4$. It is locally flat at a boundary point when there are such neighborhoods and a homeomorphism of pairs to $(\mathbb R^4_+,\mathbb R^2_+)$, where $\mathbb R^4_+=\{x_4\geq0\}$ and $\mathbb R^2_+=\{x_2=x_3=0,\ x_4\geq0\}$; the line $\partial\mathbb R^2_+$ lies in $\partial\mathbb R^4_+$. A collar of a boundary circle of $W$ is an embedding of that circle times $[0,\varepsilon)$ into $W$ that is the identity on the circle at parameter $0$; a concordance collar is required to agree with the corresponding product collar of the ambient end. A smooth proper surface has the analogous smooth charts and collars, which are also topological locally flat charts.

Let C^{1/n} be the classes under equivalence witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W with boundary the two standard endpoint 3-spheres such that each boundary inclusion induces an isomorphism H_i(S³;R_n)→H_i(W;R_n) for every i. derivations.claim: Remove the interior of A×D² from W. Its side boundary is A×S¹. Attaching D²×S¹×I with the stated slope identifications fills each endpoint exterior along its preferred longitude, so the new boundary components are M(K₀) and −M(K₁), by [F1].

The construction is functorial in the product collars and preserves the meridian classes. If π₁(W)=1, van Kampen applied to W=(W\int(A×D²))∪(A×D²) shows that the annulus-normal meridian normally generates π₁ of the exterior; this meridian lies in each zero-surgery boundary group.

The required R-homology conclusion should follow by comparing the Mayer–Vietoris sequences of W=E∪(A×D²) and V=E∪(D²×S¹×I), with the endpoint decompositions of S³ and M(K_i). The annulus framing identifies the torus maps, but the degreewise chain maps and the five-lemma comparison are not supplied in this draft.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, let $B^4=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\lVert x\rVert^2\le1\}$ with boundary $S^3$. The oriented connected sum $K\#K^\dagger$ bounds a smooth properly embedded disk $D\subset B^4$ for which the squared radial function $\rho(x)=\lVert x\rVert^2$ restricts to a Morse function on the interior of $D$ with all critical points of index $0$ or $1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. On oriented ambient-isotopy classes of smooth knots in $S^3$, the connected-sum operation is associative and commutative, and the standard unknot is a two-sided identity. Here “commutative monoid” means a set with an associative binary operation, a two-sided identity, and equality after interchanging the two inputs.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The supplied connected-sum theorem gives associativity, commutativity and the unknot identity on knot concordance classes. Taking boundary connected sums of the witnessing annuli gives the corresponding operation in the standard smooth and locally flat products.
The reverse-mirror construction in [F2] supplies an inverse annulus in the standard 4-ball, hence in the standard product, and so it is admissible in all four categories.

For C_ex and C^{1/n}, transitivity and compatibility of boundary connected sum must be checked against the specified ambient homeomorphism and R_n-homology conditions. The definitions in [F1] alone do not prove these gluing properties, and the smooth and topological arguments in steps 1.1–1.2 do not supply the missing verification.

Let V=S¹×D² be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core, meridional disk and product longitude. A pattern is a smooth oriented knot P in the interior of V. Its winding number w(P) is its algebraic intersection with an oriented meridional disk, equivalently the coefficient of the core in [P]∈H₁(V;Z). For a smooth oriented knot K in S³, let e_K:V→S³ be a zero-framed tubular embedding carrying the core to K and carrying the meridian and product longitude to the positive meridian and preferred longitude of K. The satellite knot P(K) is e_K(P).

When concordance preservation has been established, the formula [K]↦[P(K)] defines a set map on each of C_sm, C_top, C_ex and C^{1/n}. The solid-torus meridian is strong winding number ±1 for P if, after V is embedded as the standard unknotted solid torus and P(U) denotes the resulting closure, that meridian normally generates π₁(S³\P(U)). Normal generation means that the smallest normal subgroup containing the element is the whole group. Strong winding number ±1 is a separate condition from ordinary winding number ±1. No additivity or homomorphism property is part of this definition.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Let $V=S^1\times D^2$ be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core $S^1\times\{0\}$. A **pattern** is a smooth oriented knot $P$ contained in the interior of $V$, together with a chosen closed tubular neighbourhood $N(P)$ contained in the interior of $V$. Its **winding number** $w(P)$ is the integer by which the homology class $[P]$ maps to $H_1(V;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ under the isomorphism that sends the oriented core to $1$. The **pattern exterior** is $X_P=V\setminus\operatorname{int}N(P)$; its **outer torus** is $\partial V$ and its **inner torus** is $\partial N(P)$. A **companion** is a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ with a specified orientation-preserving tubular embedding $e:V\to S^3$ that sends the core to $K$ and identifies the solid-torus meridian and product longitude with the positive meridian and preferred longitude of $K$. The **satellite knot** $P(K)$ is $e(P)$, with chosen exterior $E_{P(K)}=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}e(N(P))$; the image $e(\partial V)$ is its **companion torus**. The outer torus is **incompressible** when it bounds no properly embedded disk in $X_P$ with essential boundary on $\partial V$. It is **product-parallel** to the inner torus when $X_P$ is a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with those tori as its ends. This definition alone asserts neither incompressibility nor essentiality of the companion torus.

derivations.claim: Represent K#J by placing K and J in disjoint 3-balls and joining the removed arcs by a product band. Choose the zero-framed tubular neighborhood so its meridian and preferred longitude restrict to the corresponding meridians and longitudes on both sides of the separating sphere.

Insert P into that neighborhood and cut along the separating sphere. Inside the K-ball the inserted tangle is exactly the arc of P with K tied into it, which is the pattern P_K. The remaining J-ball is the companion neighborhood for P_K(J). Gluing along the separating annulus matches the same meridian and preferred longitude, so the two constructions are related by an orientation-preserving isotopy of the glued knots.

Tying a local knot into an arc contained in a 3-ball does not change the homology class of P in the solid torus. Its core coefficient, and hence its winding number, is unchanged. This proves both claims.

derivations.claim: In the smooth product category, choose a tubular neighborhood of the smooth annulus A. Its oriented normal 2-plane bundle over A has relative Euler obstruction in H²(A,∂A;Z)≅Z. The boundary trivializations are the zero framings of K₀ and K₁; the relative obstruction is the difference of their self-linking numbers, hence zero. A relative framing therefore identifies a neighborhood of A with A×D² and agrees with the two prescribed endpoint zero-framed neighborhoods.

In that framed neighborhood insert P in every disk fiber. The result is an embedded annulus from P(K₀) to P(K₁); the product collars and endpoint framings are preserved. This proves concordance preservation for smooth annuli in a standard product.

For a locally flat annulus, the corresponding statement requires a locally flat normal-disk-neighborhood theorem with a relative trivialization matching the endpoint zero framings. That supplier is absent from the local prerequisites, and the smooth vector-bundle argument in step 1.1 does not prove its topological microbundle analogue.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle, and let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. Choose a radius $\epsilon>0$ whose closed disk subbundle $D_\epsilon\nu(K)$ is contained in $\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

derivations.claim: Let λ denote the longitude of the pattern solid torus. Filling the outer boundary of the pattern exterior along λ produces S³∖P(U), so the induced epimorphism π₁(ST∖P)→π₁(S³∖P(U)) has kernel normally generated by λ. By [F1], the target is normally generated by the image of η; hence π₁(ST∖P) is normally generated by η and λ.

For a local connected sum with any knot J, the closure-complement group is the amalgamated product of the two knot groups along their common meridian, by cutting at the connected-sum sphere and applying van Kampen. Each knot-group factor is normally generated by its meridian.

Decompose the complement of P(K) along the companion torus into ST∖P and S³∖K. Van Kampen gives a generating set normally contained in the images of these two groups. The first is normally generated by η and λ by step 1.1; the second is normally generated by μ_K by [F3].

Under the torus gluing, λ is identified with λ_K and η with μ_K. Since μ_K normally generates the companion-knot group, λ becomes redundant, and η normally generates the entire satellite-complement group. The outer solid-torus meridian for the pattern P(K) is isotopic in the complement to η, so it too normally generates.

The solid-torus meridian normally generates the strong-winding factor by hypothesis; quotienting the amalgamated product by that meridian kills this factor and the common meridian. The other knot-group factor is then killed because its meridian normally generates it. Thus the whole closure-complement group is normally generated by the solid-torus meridian.

Assume full AC, matching the chosen finite twisted-chain and maximal-abelian-cover conventions. Let K be a smooth oriented knot, M(K) its preferred-longitude zero-framed surgery, W a compact connected oriented smooth 4-manifold with boundary M(K), and π=π₁(W). Put π^(0)=π and π^(j+1)=[π^(j),π^(j)]. A right Zπ-chain complex with coefficients in a left Z[π/π^(j)]-module is formed by tensoring over Zπ with that module.

For n≥0, W is an integral n-solution for K when H₁(M(K);Z)→H₁(W;Z) is an isomorphism, H₂(W;Z) is free of rank 2r for some finite r, and there are classes x₁,…,x_r,y₁,…,y_r in H₂(W;Z[π/π^(n)]) whose equivariant intersection pairings satisfy λ_n(x_i,x_j)=0 and λ_n(x_i,y_j)=δ_ij. It is an integral (n+1/2)-solution when, in addition, each x_i is the image of a class x̃_i in H₂(W;Z[π/π^(n+1)]) and λ_{n+1}(x̃_i,x̃_j)=0 for all i,j. Here λ_j is the equivariant intersection pairing induced by the orientation of W.

For a commutative ring R with 1≠0, a group G belongs to Strebel's class D(R) if every homomorphism between projective RG-modules is injective whenever its tensor with the trivial G-module R is injective. In this page R is Q or F_p for a prime p. For a countable discrete group G, its group von Neumann algebra N G is the weak-operator closure of CG in the left regular representation on ℓ²(G), with trace τ_G(T)=⟨Tδ_e,δ_e⟩. The von Neumann dimension of a finitely generated projective N G-module represented by a projection E is τ_G(E); for an arbitrary module it is the supremum of the dimensions of its finitely generated projective submodules.

For a compact oriented 4-manifold W with boundary, sign(W) is the inertia difference of the symmetric intersection form on H₂(W;R) modulo its radical (the subspace pairing to zero with every class), equivalently on the image of H₂(W;R)→H₂(W,∂W;R). Given a closed oriented 3-manifold M, a homomorphism φ:π₁(M)→G, a compact oriented 4-manifold W with ∂W=M, and an extension ψ:π₁(W)→G of φ, the L²-signature sign_G^(2)(W,ψ) is the von Neumann signature of the nonsingular part of the N G-coefficient intersection form. When such a W and extension exist, the signature defect is sign_G^(2)(W,ψ)−sign(W). It is called the rho invariant of (M,φ) only after its independence of the bounding data is established by a separate bordism argument.

derivations.claim: Apply the bar resolution of the trivial CG-module to express the higher Tor groups as homology of a chain complex of induced modules. Amenability supplies Følner sets that make the normalized boundary-rank defects tend to zero.

Turning the Følner estimate into zero von Neumann dimension requires the dimension-continuity and approximation lemmas in Cha–Orr Theorem 6.6; neither follows from the definition of amenability alone.

For a smooth oriented knot K in S³, let e_K:V→S³ be a zero-framed tubular embedding carrying the core to K and carrying the meridian and product longitude to the positive meridian and preferred longitude of K. The satellite knot P(K) is e_K(P).

When concordance preservation has been established, the formula [K]↦[P(K)] defines a set map on each of C_sm, C_top, C_ex and C^{1/n}. The solid-torus meridian is strong winding number ±1 for P if, after V is embedded as the standard unknotted solid torus and P(U) denotes the resulting closure, that meridian normally generates π₁(S³\P(U)). Normal generation means that the smallest normal subgroup containing the element is the whole group. Strong winding number ±1 is a separate condition from ordinary winding number ±1. No additivity or homomorphism property is part of this definition.

Let P be an oriented pattern of winding n≠0 and K an oriented knot. If P(U) bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth 4-manifold B with boundary S³ and H_i(S³;R_n)→H_i(B;R_n) is an isomorphism for every i, then for every K the zero surgeries M(P(K)) and M(K) are smoothly R_n-homology cobordant, with preferred meridian carried to preferred meridian. If P has strong winding number ±1 and P(U) is pseudo-slice (respectively locally flat topologically slice), then M(P(K)) and M(K) are smoothly (respectively topologically) homology cobordant through a 4-manifold whose fundamental group is normally generated by the image of the fundamental group of either boundary component. The category and closure hypotheses are separate and cannot be inferred from winding alone.

Let knots be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented S³ and let I=[0,1]. Let C_sm be their smooth concordance classes, where equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in S³×I. Let C_top be their locally flat topological concordance classes in that product. Let C_ex be their exotic-smooth concordance classes: equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W together with an orientation-preserving homeomorphism of pairs (W,∂W)≅(S³×I,S³×{0,1}) matching the endpoint knots. For a nonzero integer n set R_n=Z[1/|n|]. Let C^{1/n} be the classes under equivalence witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W with boundary the two standard endpoint 3-spheres such that each boundary inclusion induces an isomorphism H_i(S³;R_n)→H_i(W;R_n) for every i. A knot is pseudo-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth 4-manifold homeomorphic to B⁴, with the boundary identified with the standard S³. A knot is Z[1/|n|]-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth 4-manifold whose boundary inclusion is an isomorphism on homology with coefficients R_n. These are sets of equivalence classes; this definition alone asserts no group structure.

Assume AC_ω. Under connected sum, each of C_sm, C_top, C_ex and C^{1/n} is an abelian group. The identity is the class of the unknot, and the inverse of [K] is the class of the reverse mirror of K. Each category retains the ambient and coefficient conditions in its definition.

Let B be a smooth 4-ball embedded in the standard smooth 4-sphere S⁴. The closure of S⁴\B is diffeomorphic to the standard 4-ball. This is the special smooth Schoenflies complement assertion used after a capped contractible 4-manifold has been identified with standard S⁴; it does not assert the smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture.

Let P be a pattern and let K be a knot. Form a pattern P_K by tying K into a small arc of P in a ball disjoint from the solid-torus core, using the zero framing. For every knot J, the satellite P(K#J) is isotopic as an oriented knot to P_K(J). The pattern P_K has the same winding number as P.

Let P⊂S¹×D² be a smooth oriented pattern. If oriented knots K₀ and K₁ are concordant in one of the four categories C_sm, C_top, C_ex or C^{1/n}, then P(K₀) and P(K₁) are concordant in the same category. Thus P induces a well-defined set map on each of these concordance sets.

Let A be a proper annulus in a compact oriented 4-manifold W, with boundary knots K₀ and K₁ in the two boundary 3-spheres. Assume A has an oriented normal disk neighborhood A×D² whose endpoint framings are the preferred zero-linking longitudes. Let R be Z or R_n=Z[1/|n|], and assume each end S³→W is an R-homology isomorphism. Removing A×D² and attaching D²×S¹×I along the annular side, with ∂D² matched to the annulus longitude and the core matched to the normal meridian, produces a cobordism V from M(K₀) to M(K₁). The statement predicts that the boundary inclusions M(K_i)→V are R-homology isomorphisms. If W is simply connected, it also predicts that π₁(V) is normally generated by either endpoint knot-group image.

Let P be a pattern of strong winding number ±1. For every oriented knot K, regard P(K) as the pattern obtained by tying K into each strand of P in the companion solid torus. Then this new pattern P(K) also has strong winding number ±1. A pattern obtained from any strong-winding pattern by taking connected sum with a local knot also has strong winding number ±1.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, let $B^4=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\lVert x\rVert^2\le1\}$ with boundary $S^3$. The oriented connected sum $K\#K^\dagger$ bounds a smooth properly embedded disk $D\subset B^4$ for which the squared radial function $\rho(x)=\lVert x\rVert^2$ restricts to a Morse function on the interior of $D$ with all critical points of index $0$ or $1$.

derivations.claim: Suppose P(K)=P(U), with the stated closure-slice hypothesis. By [F7] this equality is witnessed by a concordance annulus; [F8] gives a meridian-preserving homology cobordism from M(P(K)) to M(P(U)). Applying [F2] to K and U gives cobordisms from M(P(K)) to M(K) and from M(P(U)) to M(U).

Glue the cobordisms along the identified surgery manifolds. Mayer–Vietoris shows that the resulting boundary inclusions retain the required homology isomorphisms. In the exotic/topological branches, van Kampen shows the boundary normal-generation condition is preserved under this gluing. Hence M(K) and M(U) satisfy the corresponding surgery-cobordism relation.

In the localized category, cap the M(U)=S¹×S² end with S¹×B³ and attach a 2-handle along the meridian. The resulting 4-manifold has boundary S³ and is an R_n-homology ball; the 2-handle co-core is a smooth disk bounded by K. Thus K=U in C^{1/n}.

In the exotic and topological categories, the normal-generation condition makes the capped manifold after the meridian 2-handle contractible with boundary S³. Its co-core is a smooth disk in the exotic branch and a locally flat disk in the topological branch once the resulting contractible manifold is homeomorphic to B⁴. That relative Freedman implication is the missing supplier recorded below.

In the ordinary smooth branch, if P(U) is smoothly slice and P has strong winding ±1, the same cap and handle construction gives a contractible smooth 4-manifold B with boundary S³. Capping B with standard B⁴ gives a smooth homotopy S⁴; under the smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture and [F5], B is diffeomorphic to B⁴.

Now suppose P(K)=P(J). By [F6], P(J)=P_K(−K#J). Define R as the local connected sum of −P(K) with P_K. Then R(−K#J) is concordant to U because K#(−K#J) is concordant to J and satellites preserve concordance; moreover R(U)=−P(K)#P(K). By [F10], this closure is ribbon; [F6] gives w(R)=w(P).

If P has strong winding ±1, [F9] implies R also has strong winding ±1. The closure R(U) supplies the localized slice, pseudo-slice, topological-slice, and standard smooth-slice hypotheses in their respective branches. Apply the applicable earlier weak-injectivity branch to R to obtain K#(−J)=U and hence K=J.

Let $M$ be a closed oriented three-manifold with a specified coefficient homomorphism $\phi:\pi_1(M_j)\to\Gamma$ on each component, where $\Gamma$ is PTFA. The integral coefficient ring is $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[\Gamma]$ with its fraction division ring $K\Gamma$. More generally let $k$ be $\mathbb Z$ or a commutative field, let $K$ be the fraction division ring of $k[\Gamma]$, and let $k[\Gamma]\subseteq R\subseteq K$ be an involution-stable unital intermediate ring. The involution fixes $k$ and sends $g$ to $g^{-1}$; on fractions it is the involutive anti-automorphism extending this formula. Taking $k=\mathbb Z$ and $R=\Lambda$ recovers the integral convention.

If $H_1(M;K)=0$, the coefficient Bockstein, oriented Poincaré duality and evaluation define the Blanchfield linking pairing
$$B_{M,\phi,R}:TH_1(M;R)\times TH_1(M;R)\longrightarrow K/R.$$

The integral coefficient ring is $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[\Gamma]$ with its fraction division ring $K\Gamma$. More generally let $k$ be $\mathbb Z$ or a commutative field, let $K$ be the fraction division ring of $k[\Gamma]$, and let $k[\Gamma]\subseteq R\subseteq K$ be an involution-stable unital intermediate ring. The involution fixes $k$ and sends $g$ to $g^{-1}$; on fractions it is the involutive anti-automorphism extending this formula. Taking $k=\mathbb Z$ and $R=\Lambda$ recovers the integral convention.

If $H_1(M;K)=0$, the coefficient Bockstein, oriented Poincaré duality and evaluation define the Blanchfield linking pairing
$$B_{M,\phi,R}:TH_1(M;R)\times TH_1(M;R)\longrightarrow K/R.$$
Here $T$ denotes the submodule of elements with a nonzero right annihilator, the first variable is conjugate-linear, and the second is right-linear. Nonsingularity means that the adjoint
$$\overline{TH_1(M;R)}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_R(TH_1(M;R),K/R)$$
is an isomorphism of left $R$-modules, where $r\cdot\bar x=\overline{x\bar r}$ on the conjugate module. This is equivalent to the conjugate-dual formulation in the right-module convention. For a homomorphism φ:π₁(M)→G and an extension ψ:π₁(W)→G over a compact oriented 4-manifold W with ∂W=M, define the signature defect by ρ(M,φ;W,ψ)=sign_G^(2)(W,ψ)−sign(W). It is an invariant of (M,φ) only when a separate bordism-independence theorem applies.

Let $\Gamma$ be PTFA and let $k$ be either $\mathbb Z$ or a commutative field. The group ring $A=k[\Gamma]$ has no zero divisors, satisfies both Ore conditions, and has a fraction division ring $K$ in which every element is both a right and a left fraction of elements of $A$. The involution $\overline{\sum c_g g}=\sum c_g g^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive anti-automorphism of $K$.

Every intermediate unital ring $A\subseteq R\subseteq K$ has no zero divisors, satisfies both Ore conditions, and has this same $K$ as its fraction division ring. If $R$ is stable under the extended involution, that involution restricts to $R$ and descends to its additive quotient $K/R$. None of these assertions requires a choice principle.

Let $R$ be a unital ring with $1\ne0$ and no zero divisors. Suppose both Ore conditions hold: any two nonzero elements have a nonzero common right multiple and a nonzero common left multiple. Let $R\subseteq K$ be a unital embedding into a division ring such that every element of $K$ is a right fraction $as^{-1}$ with $a\in R$ and $0\ne s\in R$.

For every right $R$-module $M$, the right $K$-module $M\otimes_RK$ is represented by fractions $[m,s]$ with $m\in M$ and $0\ne s\in R$, corresponding to $m\otimes s^{-1}$. The equality criterion is
$$[m,s]=[n,t]\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{there exist }0\ne u,v\in R\text{ with }su=tv\text{ and }mu=nv.$$
In particular, $[m,s]=0$ if and only if $ma=0$ for some $0\ne a\in R$. Thus the kernel of $M\to M\otimes_RK$, $m\mapsto m\otimes1$, is exactly the set of elements with a nonzero right annihilator, and $M\otimes_RK=0$ if and only if every element of $M$ has a nonzero right annihilator.

The functor $-\otimes_RK$ is exact on arbitrary right $R$-modules, so $K$ is flat as a left $R$-module. For every chain complex $C_\bullet$ of right $R$-modules, the canonical map gives a natural isomorphism
$$H_i(C_\bullet)\otimes_RK\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }H_i(C_\bullet\otimes_RK)$$
for every integer $i$. No finite-generation, finite-presentation or boundedness assumption on the modules or complexes is required.

The corresponding left-module assertions also hold: $K$ is flat as a right $R$-module, $1\otimes m$ is zero in $K\otimes_RM$ precisely when $am=0$ for some $0\ne a\in R$, and $K\otimes_R-$ commutes with the homology of arbitrary left-module chain complexes. All assertions require no choice axiom.

Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff manifold, $o\in M$, and $R$ a unital ring. One can construct paths $\gamma_x$ from $o$ to every $x\in M$, with $\gamma_o$ constant, by fixed rules from one finite atlas and finitely many connecting paths. Let $\mathcal R$ be a right-$R$ local system with a supplied identification $\mathcal R_o=R$ and transport given by left multiplication by units, with monodromy image $H\le R^\times$. Its twisted singular complex has an explicit chain decomposition $C_*(M;\mathcal R)=C'_*\oplus Q_*$ after a change of free bases, where $C'_0=R$, $C'_* $ is free, and $Q_*$ is contractible with its only nonzero differential an identity from degree one to degree zero. Moreover
$$\operatorname{im}(d'_1)=\sum_{h\in H}(h-1)R.$$
The decomposition and its dual cochain homotopy equivalences require no choice principle. In particular this image is principal if $H$ is cyclic, if it equals $R$, or if every right ideal of $R$ is principal.

Let $R$ be an associative unital ring with $1\ne0$ and no zero divisors, embedded as a unital subring in a division ring $K$, put $N=K/R$ as a right $R$-module, and let $C_*$ be a right $R$-module chain complex concentrated in nonnegative degrees. Supply an identification $C_0=R$. If the right ideal $\operatorname{im}(d_1)$ is principal, restriction to cycles gives an isomorphism
$$H^1(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,N))\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_1(C_*),N).$$
Neither a principal ideal domain hypothesis on $R$ nor a choice principle is required.

Let $(M,o)$ be a compact connected based Hausdorff manifold, let $R$ be an involutive unital ring, and supply a rank-one right-$R$ local system $\mathcal R$ with an identification $\mathcal R_o=R$. Assume every based-loop monodromy is left multiplication by a unit $u$ satisfying $\bar u=u^{-1}$. Equip the base fiber with the standard Hermitian form $h_o(a,b)=\bar a b$. Transport extends this to a path-independent parallel Hermitian form $h$ on $\mathcal R$. Put $C_*=C_*(M;\mathcal R)$. For a right $R$-module $P$, write $\overline P$ for its conjugate left module, with $r\cdot\bar p=\overline{p\bar r}$.

The left-$R$ cochain complex $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R)$ is the intrinsic cochain complex of the left-$R$ local system with fiber $R$ and transport $a\mapsto au^{-1}$. Relative to the supplied parallel Hermitian form, that local system is naturally isomorphic to $\overline{\mathcal R}$ by $\bar v\mapsto[w\mapsto h(v,w)]$. The identifications are independent of unitary fiber frames; an arbitrary change of Hermitian structure is not asserted to preserve them. If $M$ is oriented, boundaryless and of dimension $n$, cap duality therefore gives
$$H^p(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R))\cong\overline{H_{n-p}(C_*)}.$$
If $R\subseteq K$ is an embedding into an involutive division ring extending the involution, the same conclusion is valid for $K$, with $C_*\otimes_R K$ in the homology target. If $R$ is involution-stable in $K$, the complex $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,K/R)$ is the corresponding intrinsic left-$R$ cochain complex with fiber $K/R$ and transport by right multiplication by $u^{-1}$. These identifications require no choice principle and commute with the coefficient maps $R\to K\to K/R$.

Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff manifold with a basepoint, and let $0\to\mathcal A\xrightarrow{i}\mathcal B\xrightarrow{q}\mathcal C\to0$ be a short exact sequence of local systems of abelian groups on $M$. There is a natural coefficient Bockstein making the sequence
$$H^1(M;\mathcal B)\xrightarrow{q_*}H^1(M;\mathcal C)\xrightarrow{\beta}H^2(M;\mathcal A)\xrightarrow{i_*}H^2(M;\mathcal B)$$
exact at its two middle terms. In particular $\beta$ is an isomorphism if $H^1(M;\mathcal B)=H^2(M;\mathcal B)=0$. No choice principle is assumed. If the local systems and maps have a commuting coefficient-ring action, the sequence and Bockstein respect it.

derivations.claim: Work first on one nonempty connected component. Put $C_*=C_*(M;R)$ in the right-module convention. By [F2], $R$ has no zero divisors, satisfies both Ore conditions, and has fraction division ring $K$. The supplied homomorphism has unitary transport units for the given involution. By [F4], replace $C_*$ by its explicitly homotopy equivalent free complex $C'_*$ with $C'_0=R$. This replacement preserves homology, dual cohomology and the natural evaluation maps; the discarded summand has an explicitly contracted identity differential.

By [F3] and $H_1(M;K)=0$, one has $H_1(C_*)\otimes_RK=0$. The elementwise zero criterion of [F3] says that every element of $H_1(C_*)$ has a nonzero right annihilator. Thus the whole module equals its torsion submodule. This uses arbitrary-complex localization, so no finite CW or triangulation assumption is introduced.

The degree-zero term of $C'_*\otimes_RK$ is $K$, and the image of its degree-one differential is either zero or $K$. In the first case $d_1=0$, and $H_1(M;K)=0$ implies that every degree-one chain is a boundary, so every degree-one dual cocycle vanishes. In the second case choose $z$ with $d_1z=1$; then $C'_1\otimes_RK=\ker d_1\oplus zK$. The same homology vanishing says $\ker d_1=\operatorname{im}d_2$, so every dual cocycle factors through $d_1$ and is the coboundary of its value on $z$. Hence $H^1(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,K))=0$, using the tensor adjunction in [F5]. Also [F5] directly identifies $H^2(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,K))$ with $\overline{H_1(M;K)}=0$. The exact segment [F6], applied to the compatible dual local systems of [F5], therefore gives a Bockstein isomorphism $\beta:H^1(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,K/R))\to H^2(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R))$.

Restriction of a cocycle to cycles always defines the left-$R$ linear evaluation map $\kappa:H^1(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,K/R))\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_1(C_*),K/R)$. Under the additional alternatives it is an isomorphism by [F4]. Indeed the reduced boundary image $B_0\subseteq C'_0=R$ is a right ideal, so it is principal if $R$ is right principal. If $H_0(M;R)=0$, it is all of $R$. If the coefficient image is cyclic generated by $t$, it is $(t-1)R$, including zero for trivial image. These verify precisely the hypothesis of the principal-boundary evaluation lemma, whose proof allows arbitrary $C'_1$. Thus no finite generation or principal-ideal assumption is silently imposed in the other two branches.

By [F5], the inverse oriented duality map is an isomorphism $\overline{H_1(C_*)}\to H^2(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R))$. Compose it with $\beta^{-1}$ from step 2.2 and the evaluation map $\kappa$ from step 2.3. Evaluating the resulting functional on $y$ defines $B(x,y)\in K/R$. The composition is left-$R$ linear on the conjugate module and its values are right-$R$ linear functions of $y$, so $B(xr,y)=\bar rB(x,y)$ and $B(x,ys)=B(x,y)s$. This is exactly [F1]'s Bockstein–duality pairing, defined before any claim that $\kappa$ is invertible. Under the alternatives of step 2.3, all three maps in its adjoint are isomorphisms. Therefore $\overline{H_1(C_*)}\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_1(C_*),K/R)$ is an isomorphism, which is nonsingularity in the stated right-module convention.

A compact manifold has finitely many components, since its connected components are open and cover it. Apply the argument to each, using only finitely many basepoint and finite-atlas choices. Chains split over those components, and cochains are a finite product, so their cycle/boundary and Bockstein decompositions need no infinite primitive selection. The oriented fundamental class is the sum of the component classes, and the pairing is their orthogonal direct sum. Under the stated componentwise alternatives, each adjoint is an isomorphism, hence so is their finite direct sum. Empty $M$ gives the unique pairing on the zero module. In particular a cyclic integral coefficient image satisfies the third alternative even when $R=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$ is not right principal. This proves the full stated scope without a choice axiom.

For a commutative ring R with 1≠0, a group G belongs to Strebel's class D(R) if every homomorphism between projective RG-modules is injective whenever its tensor with the trivial G-module R is injective. For a compact oriented 4-manifold W with boundary, sign(W) is the inertia difference of the symmetric intersection form on H₂(W;R) modulo its radical (the subspace pairing to zero with every class), equivalently on the image of H₂(W;R)→H₂(W,∂W;R). Given a closed oriented 3-manifold M, a homomorphism φ:π₁(M)→G, a compact oriented 4-manifold W with ∂W=M, and an extension ψ:π₁(W)→G of φ, the L²-signature sign_G^(2)(W,ψ) is the von Neumann signature of the nonsingular part of the N G-coefficient intersection form. When such a W and extension exist, the signature defect is sign_G^(2)(W,ψ)−sign(W). It is called the rho invariant of (M,φ) only after its independence of the bounding data is established by a separate bordism argument.

Let W₀ and W₁ be compact oriented smooth 4-manifolds with a common identified boundary M, and let Γ be a discrete group. Suppose coefficient homomorphisms ψ_i:π₁(W_i)→Γ agree on π₁(M), and let X=W₀∪_M(−W₁) be the resulting closed oriented 4-manifold with its glued coefficient map. Then
sign(X)=sign(W₀)−sign(W₁)
and
sign_Γ^(2)(X)=sign_Γ^(2)(W₀,ψ₀)−sign_Γ^(2)(W₁,ψ₁).

Let X be a closed oriented smooth 4-manifold, Γ a discrete group, and φ:π₁(X)→Γ a homomorphism. Then the von Neumann signature of the NΓ-coefficient intersection form equals the ordinary signature:
sign_Γ^(2)(X,φ)=sign(X).

derivations.claim: Glue W₀ to −W₁ along their identified boundary M. The boundary representations agree, so ψ₀ and ψ₁ glue to a homomorphism on the fundamental group of the closed oriented 4-manifold X=W₀∪_M(−W₁).
Novikov additivity for the ordinary signature and for the von Neumann signature gives sign(X)=sign(W₀)−sign(W₁) and sign_Γ^(2)(X)=sign_Γ^(2)(W₀,ψ₀)−sign_Γ^(2)(W₁,ψ₁).
By [F3], the two closed signatures in step 2.1 are equal. Rearranging yields equality of the two signature defects.

Let V=S¹×D² be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core, meridional disk and product longitude. A pattern is a smooth oriented knot P in the interior of V. Its winding number w(P) is its algebraic intersection with an oriented meridional disk, equivalently the coefficient of the core in [P]∈H₁(V;Z). For a smooth oriented knot K in S³, let e_K:V→S³ be a zero-framed tubular embedding carrying the core to K and carrying the meridian and product longitude to the positive meridian and preferred longitude of K. The satellite knot P(K) is e_K(P).

When concordance preservation has been established, the formula [K]↦[P(K)] defines a set map on each of C_sm, C_top, C_ex and C^{1/n}. The solid-torus meridian is strong winding number ±1 for P if, after V is embedded as the standard unknotted solid torus and P(U) denotes the resulting closure, that meridian normally generates π₁(S³\P(U)). Normal generation means that the smallest normal subgroup containing the element is the whole group. Strong winding number ±1 is a separate condition from ordinary winding number ±1. No additivity or homomorphism property is part of this definition.

Let knots be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented S³ and let I=[0,1]. Let C_sm be their smooth concordance classes, where equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in S³×I. Let C_top be their locally flat topological concordance classes in that product. Let C_ex be their exotic-smooth concordance classes: equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W together with an orientation-preserving homeomorphism of pairs (W,∂W)≅(S³×I,S³×{0,1}) matching the endpoint knots. For a nonzero integer n set R_n=Z[1/|n|]. Let C^{1/n} be the classes under equivalence witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W with boundary the two standard endpoint 3-spheres such that each boundary inclusion induces an isomorphism H_i(S³;R_n)→H_i(W;R_n) for every i. A knot is pseudo-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth 4-manifold homeomorphic to B⁴, with the boundary identified with the standard S³. A knot is Z[1/|n|]-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth 4-manifold whose boundary inclusion is an isomorphism on homology with coefficients R_n. These are sets of equivalence classes; this definition alone asserts no group structure.

Let P be a pattern of nonzero winding n. If P(U) is smoothly slice in an R_n-homology 4-ball, then P is weakly injective on C^{1/n}, meaning P(K)=P(U) implies K=U in that category. If P has strong winding number ±1 and P(U) is pseudo-slice (respectively locally flat topologically slice), then P is weakly injective on C_ex (respectively C_top). In ordinary smooth concordance, if P(U) is smoothly slice in standard B⁴ and P has strong winding number ±1, then P is weakly injective on C_sm provided the smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture holds.

For any pattern P and knots K,J with P(K)=P(J) in one of these concordance groups, the connected-sum reduction constructs a pattern R for which R(−K#J) is concordant to U, whose closure R(U)=−P(K)#P(K) is ribbon, and whose winding w(R)=w(P). If P is strong winding ±1, then R is strong winding ±1. This reduction turns injectivity of P into weak injectivity of R; it does not assert that P itself is weakly injective without the closure hypotheses above.

Assume AC_ω. Under connected sum, each of C_sm, C_top, C_ex and C^{1/n} is an abelian group. The identity is the class of the unknot, and the inverse of [K] is the class of the reverse mirror of K. Each category retains the ambient and coefficient conditions in its definition.

Let P⊂S¹×D² be a smooth oriented pattern. If oriented knots K₀ and K₁ are concordant in one of the four categories C_sm, C_top, C_ex or C^{1/n}, then P(K₀) and P(K₁) are concordant in the same category. Thus P induces a well-defined set map on each of these concordance sets.

Let B be a smooth 4-ball embedded in the standard smooth 4-sphere S⁴. The closure of S⁴\B is diffeomorphic to the standard 4-ball. This is the special smooth Schoenflies complement assertion used after a capped contractible 4-manifold has been identified with standard S⁴; it does not assert the smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture.

derivations.claim: Suppose P(K)=P(J) as concordance classes. By [F5] these values are defined in the chosen category, and the group law gives −[P(K)]#[P(J)]=0.
Apply the auxiliary-pattern reduction [F3] to obtain R with R(−K#J)=U, closure R(U)=−P(K)#P(K) ribbon, and winding w(R)=w(P).
If P has strong winding ±1, [F3] preserves strong winding for R; in the localized branch R has the same nonzero winding.
The weak-injectivity part of [F3] applies to R and yields K#(−J)=U, hence K=J. In ordinary smooth concordance the last step uses [F6] and assumes uniqueness of the smooth structure on S⁴.

Let $M$ be a closed oriented three-manifold with a specified coefficient homomorphism $\phi:\pi_1(M_j)\to\Gamma$ on each component, where $\Gamma$ is PTFA. The integral coefficient ring is $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[\Gamma]$ with its fraction division ring $K\Gamma$. More generally let $k$ be $\mathbb Z$ or a commutative field, let $K$ be the fraction division ring of $k[\Gamma]$, and let $k[\Gamma]\subseteq R\subseteq K$ be an involution-stable unital intermediate ring. The involution fixes $k$ and sends $g$ to $g^{-1}$; on fractions it is the involutive anti-automorphism extending this formula. Taking $k=\mathbb Z$ and $R=\Lambda$ recovers the integral convention.

If $H_1(M;K)=0$, the coefficient Bockstein, oriented Poincaré duality and evaluation define the Blanchfield linking pairing
$$B_{M,\phi,R}:TH_1(M;R)\times TH_1(M;R)\longrightarrow K/R.$$
Here $T$ denotes the submodule of elements with a nonzero right annihilator, the first variable is conjugate-linear, and the second is right-linear. Nonsingularity means that the adjoint
$$\overline{TH_1(M;R)}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_R(TH_1(M;R),K/R)$$
is an isomorphism of left $R$-modules, where $r\cdot\bar x=\overline{x\bar r}$ on the conjugate module. This is equivalent to the conjugate-dual formulation in the right-module convention. For $\Gamma=\mathbb Z$ with generator $t$, $R=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$ and $K=\mathbb Q(t)$ give the classical coefficient convention. Nonsingularity is a separate property of the defined pairing, with its coefficient hypotheses supplied by the nonsingularity theorem.

For a homomorphism φ:π₁(M)→G and an extension ψ:π₁(W)→G over a compact oriented 4-manifold W with ∂W=M, define the signature defect by ρ(M,φ;W,ψ)=sign_G^(2)(W,ψ)−sign(W). It is an invariant of (M,φ) only when a separate bordism-independence theorem applies.

Let P be a winding-zero pattern satisfying the nonzero Blanchfield self-pairing hypothesis of Cha–Kim, and let K be an arbitrary knot. The iterated infection cobordism used in the proof of Cha–Kim Theorems A and B is an integral (n+1/2)-solution for the coefficient system specified there; its higher-order Blanchfield pairing is nonsingular and its metabolizer is represented by the infection curves.

Let K be a knot and W an integral (n+1/2)-solution for M(K). Let R be Q or F_p, let G be an amenable group in Strebel's class D(R) with G^(n+1)={e}, and let φ:π₁(M(K))→G extend over W. Assume φ sends a meridian of K to an infinite-order element of G. Then the rho invariant ρ(M(K),φ) vanishes.

Assume the winding-zero and nonzero axis Blanchfield self-pairing hypotheses of Cha–Kim. For each finite stage of their iterated-infection construction, the companion knots can be chosen so that the relevant higher-order rho contribution has a fixed sign and dominates the sum of all remaining terms, using a uniform Cheeger–Gromov bound and signature functions supported near selected Alexander roots. Pairwise-coprime Alexander hypotheses are used only for the separate Theorem C separation argument, not for Theorems A or B.

derivations.claim: For n=0, Cha–Kim choose companions with signature jumps near the unit-circle root detected by the nonzero classical self-pairing. The resulting classical signature homomorphism separates infinitely many cosets in the first graded quotient.

For n≥1, construct the iterated infection cobordism from [F2]. The amenable coefficient systems and the signature-vanishing constraints in [F3] show that any putative finite relation among the selected iterates has a nonzero rho contribution.

Choose the finite companion family using [F4]. Its designated signature jumps dominate the bounded rho terms, so no nontrivial integral combination can vanish in the relevant quotient. This yields infinite rank at each stage.

The non-homomorphism conclusion follows from Cha–Kim’s separate construction showing Pⁿ(K#J) is not concordant to Pⁿ(K)#Pⁿ(J) for a chosen pair when n≥1; this uses the same nonzero-pairing hypothesis but is not implied by infinite rank alone.

derivations.claim: A cochain $f:C_1\to N$ is a cocycle precisely when $f(B_1)=0$. Restricting to $Z_1$ therefore induces a map $H_1=Z_1/B_1\to N$. A coboundary $g d_1$ vanishes on $Z_1$, so this induces the stated well-defined map $\kappa$. It is onto if every map $Z_1\to N$ vanishing on $B_1$ extends to $C_1$. It is injective if every map $B_0\to N$ extends to $C_0$: indeed a cocycle restricting to zero on $Z_1$ factors uniquely through $d_1:C_1\to B_0$, and such an extension expresses it as a coboundary.

For the principal-right-ideal alternative, $N$ is right divisible: given $n=q+R\in N$ and $0\ne a\in R$, the element $q a^{-1}+R$ multiplied on the right by $a$ equals $n$. We prove by induction on $m$ that any right-linear map $f:S\to N$ from any right submodule $S\subseteq R^m$ extends to $R^m$. For $m=0$ this is immediate. Let the projection of $S$ to the last coordinate be the right ideal $J$. If $J=0$, apply induction on the first $m-1$ coordinates and give the last basis vector value zero. Otherwise write $J=aR$ with $a\ne0$ and take $z=(z',a)\in S$. Then $S=S'\oplus zR$, where $S'=S\cap(R^{m-1}\times0)$: subtract $zr$ from an element with last coordinate $ar$, and uniqueness follows from the absence of zero divisors.

If $H_0=0$, then $d_1:C_1\to C_0$ is onto. Lift the finitely many given basis vectors of $C_0$ and extend linearly to a section $s:C_0\to C_1$. This gives $C_1=Z_1\oplus s(C_0)$. Extend a map from $Z_1$ by zero on the second summand to prove surjectivity in step 1.1. Here $B_0=C_0$, so the extension required for injectivity is automatic. The section uses only finitely many selections.

Extend $f|_{S'}$ to $g:R^{m-1}\to N$ by induction. Right divisibility supplies $v\in N$ with $va=f(z)-g(z')$. Define the extension on $R^m$ by $(u,r)\mapsto g(u)+vr$. It agrees with $f$ on $S'$ and on $z$, hence on all of $S$. This completes the finite induction, using one ideal generator, one lift, and one division at each of finitely many stages. It does not use a maximal extension argument or an infinite family of choices.

Apply the extension result of step 2.2 first to $Z_1\subseteq C_1$ and then to $B_0\subseteq C_0$, using the supplied finite bases. These are exactly the surjectivity and injectivity requirements of step 1.1. The first alternative was established in step 2.1, so $\kappa$ is an isomorphism in either case. Restriction and passage to cycles commute with every compatible left coefficient action; thus the inverse, being unique, also respects that action.

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair and $\mathcal L$ a left $R$-module local system on $X$. The cellular local chain complex computes singular local homology:
$$H_n\bigl(C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H_n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$
The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms. Intrinsically,
$$C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\cong H_n(X^n\cup A,X^{n-1}\cup A;\mathcal L).$$
If a basepoint and one oriented lift of each cell outside $A$ are supplied on every component, the $n$th group is the direct sum of the corresponding coefficient fibers, and its boundary is the signed $R[\pi]$ incidence matrix acting through monodromy.

derivations.claim: The group $\Gamma$ is torsion-free abelian, hence PTFA with its one-step series. The ring $\Lambda$ is a commutative domain: after multiplying nonzero Laurent polynomials by monomials, lexicographically leading nonzero terms of ordinary polynomials have nonzero product over $\mathbb Z$. Its fraction field is $K$. Give each circle its one-vertex, one-edge cell structure, use their eight product cells on $T^3$, and lift them to the oriented coordinate cells of $\mathbb R^3$. Opposite faces differ by $x,y,1$, respectively. Thus [F1] identifies the coefficient complex with the exterior algebra on $e_1,e_2,e_3$, with differential the graded derivation $d(e_1)=a$, $d(e_2)=b$, $d(e_3)=0$. In particular $d_1(u,v,w)=au+bv$ and $d_2(p,q,r)=(-bp,ap,aq+br)$ in the ordered bases $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(e_1\wedge e_2,e_1\wedge e_3,e_2\wedge e_3)$.

Evaluation at $x=1$ identifies $\Lambda/(a)$ with the domain $\mathbb Z[y^{\pm1}]$; its kernel is exactly $(a)$ by multiplying by a power of $x$ and applying the ordinary identity $x^j-1=(x-1)(1+\cdots+x^{j-1})$. If $au+bv=0$, reduction modulo $a$ gives $b\bar v=0$, whence $v=at$ and $u=-bt$. Therefore every degree-one cycle has a unique expression $(-bt,at,w)$. The image of $d_2$ consists precisely of those expressions with arbitrary $t=p$ and $w\in I$. Consequently $H_1(M;\Lambda)\cong\Lambda/I\cong\mathbb Z$, generated by the third circle. It is nonzero, and all of it is $\Lambda$-torsion because $a\ne0$ annihilates it.

Over $K$, multiplication by $a$ is invertible. The operator $h(\omega)=a^{-1}e_1\wedge\omega$ satisfies $dh+hd=1$ by the displayed graded-derivation differential. Hence the entire coefficient chain complex over $K$ is contractible and in particular $H_1(M;K)=0$. This verifies the vanishing assumption of the refuted statement without any finiteness or rank inference.

Any $\Lambda$-linear map $\Lambda/I\to K/\Lambda$ is determined by the image $q+\Lambda$ of $1+I$, where $aq,bq\in\Lambda$. Set $r=aq$ and $s=bq$. Then $br=as$. Reducing this identity modulo $a$ and using the domain $\Lambda/(a)$ from step 2.1 gives $r=at$ for some $t\in\Lambda$. Since $a\ne0$ in the field $K$, the identity $aq=at$ forces $q=t\in\Lambda$. Thus the image of $1+I$ is zero, and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Lambda}(\Lambda/I,K/\Lambda)=0$. The conjugate dual is also zero; the involution $x\mapsto x^{-1},y\mapsto y^{-1}$ preserves $I$ because $x^{-1}-1=-x^{-1}a$ and $y^{-1}-1=-y^{-1}b$.

By steps 2.1 and 3.1, the adjoint of any sesquilinear pairing on $TH_1(M;\Lambda)$ with target $K/\Lambda$ has nonzero source and zero target, and therefore is not an isomorphism. This includes the coefficient Bockstein–duality pairing whenever expressed in those conventions. Together with step 2.2 this refutes the asserted implication. Every object and calculation is explicit and finite; no choice assumption is needed.

Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff manifold, $o\in M$, and $R$ a unital ring. One can construct paths $\gamma_x$ from $o$ to every $x\in M$, with $\gamma_o$ constant, by fixed rules from one finite atlas and finitely many connecting paths. Let $\mathcal R$ be a right-$R$ local system with a supplied identification $\mathcal R_o=R$ and transport given by left multiplication by units, with monodromy image $H\le R^\times$. Its twisted singular complex has an explicit chain decomposition $C_*(M;\mathcal R)=C'_*\oplus Q_*$ after a change of free bases, where $C'_0=R$, $C'_* $ is free, and $Q_*$ is contractible with its only nonzero differential an identity from degree one to degree zero. Moreover
$$\operatorname{im}(d'_1)=\sum_{h\in H}(h-1)R.$$
The decomposition and its dual cochain homotopy equivalences require no choice principle. In particular this image is principal if $H$ is cyclic, if it equals $R$, or if every right ideal of $R$ is principal.

Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff topological manifold and $o\in M$. There is a finite based graph mapped continuously into $M$ such that its induced fundamental-group map is onto. Consequently $\pi_1(M,o)$ has a finite generating list, without a choice principle. No triangulation or smooth structure on $M$ is assumed.

Let $\mathcal L$ be a left $R$-module local system on $X$ and let $A\subseteq X$. Since the differentials square to zero by [[lem-twisted-boundaries-square-to-zero-and-are-independent-of-lift-bases]], define
$$H_n(X,A;\mathcal L)=H_n\bigl(C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr),\qquad H^n(X,A;\mathcal L)=H^n\bigl(C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr),$$
using the relative complexes of [[def-singular-and-cellular-chain-complexes-with-local-coefficients]]. Write $H_n(X;\mathcal L)$ and $H^n(X;\mathcal L)$ when $A=\varnothing$. Negative-degree groups are zero.

For a connected CW pair, the universal-cover tensor and equivariant-Hom models in the same definition compute these groups once their chain comparison is established below. The intrinsic definition itself applies to arbitrary spaces and never assumes that a universal cover exists. On a disconnected space, chains and homology split as direct sums over components, while cochains form the degreewise product complex described in the preceding definition. Its cohomology is, by definition, the quotient of the kernel by the image in that product complex. No identification with the product of the component cohomology groups is asserted in ZF: surjectivity of that comparison can require simultaneously choosing componentwise primitives.

If $\underline M$ is the constant system with fiber an $R$-module $M$, every transport in the intrinsic formulas is the identity. Sending $m\sigma$ to the ordinary coefficient chain and reading a cochain as an arbitrary simplex function gives literal chain and cochain isomorphisms
$$C_*(X,A;\underline M)\cong C_*(X,A;M),\qquad C^*(X,A;\underline M)\cong C^*(X,A;M).$$
Thus constant local coefficients recover ordinary singular homology and cohomology with coefficients in $M$, including empty spaces, zero coefficients, points, and relative pairs.

derivations.claim: Fix the paths from [F1]. For a degree-one cocycle $\alpha$ in a local system $\mathcal E$, the two-simplex identity of [F2] gives $\alpha(uv)=\alpha(u)+T_u^{-1}\alpha(v)$ for concatenated paths, with the second term transported to the initial fiber. A triangle realizing the concatenation proves this formula, and a triangulated homotopy square proves invariance for endpoint-fixed path homotopies; common internal edges cancel with their inverse transports. A constant two-simplex shows that a cocycle evaluates to zero on a constant path, and the concatenation formula then handles reversed paths. Define a zero-cochain $v_x=T_{\gamma_x}\alpha(\gamma_x)$ and $v_o=0$. The normalized cocycle $\alpha^0=\alpha-\delta v$ vanishes on every $\gamma_x$. If $g_\sigma=[\gamma_x\sigma\overline\gamma_y]$ for a path $\sigma:x\to y$, the concatenation formula consequently gives $\alpha^0(\sigma)=T_{\gamma_x}d(g_\sigma)$, where $d(g)=\alpha^0(g)$ on based loops. Here $d(gh)=d(g)+\rho(g)d(h)$ with $\rho(g)=T_g^{-1}$ in the cohomological convention. This is a crossed homomorphism; conversely that formula assigns a normalized cocycle to every such $d$, since the three edges of a singular two-simplex satisfy the same loop relation.

Apply step 1.1 to a $\mathcal C$-cocycle. Choose one lift $b_s\in\mathcal B_o$ of $d(s)$ for each of the finitely many generators $s$ of $\pi_1(M,o)$ from [F1]. For its inverse use $b_{s^{-1}}=-\rho(s^{-1})b_s$. Order the finite alphabet and use shortlex order on its finite words. Every group element $g$ has a least representing word $w(g)$; the identity has the empty word. On a word $t_1\cdots t_k$ form the finite sum $D(w)=\sum_j\rho(t_1\cdots t_{j-1})b_{t_j}$ in $\mathcal B_o$, and put $Q(g)=D(w(g))$. Its image in $\mathcal C_o$ is $d(g)$ by the crossed-homomorphism law. Thus $b(\sigma)=T_{\gamma_x}^{\mathcal B}Q(g_\sigma)$ gives an actual $\mathcal B$-valued one-cochain lifting $\alpha^0$ on every singular path, without selecting a fraction representative for each path. Its coboundary has zero $\mathcal C$-image, so unique inverse images under the injective fiber maps $i$ define a two-cochain $a$ in $\mathcal A$ with $i(a)=\delta b$. It is a cocycle since $i$ is injective and $\delta^2b=0$. Define $\beta[\alpha]=[a]$.

Any other lift of the same normalized one-cochain differs from $b$ by the image of a unique $\mathcal A$-valued one-cochain, so its coboundary gives the same class $[a]$. This includes changes in the finite generators, their lifts and the shortlex order. If $\alpha$ is changed by $\delta c$ for a $\mathcal C$ zero-cochain, its normalization changes by $\delta\widehat c$, where $\widehat c_x=T_{\gamma_x}c_o$: indeed the change in the normalizing zero-cochain is $c_x-T_{\gamma_x}c_o$. A single lift of $c_o$ in $\mathcal B_o$, transported along all $\gamma_x$, lifts $\widehat c$. Its coboundary adjusts $b$ without changing $\delta b$. Thus $\beta$ depends only on the cohomology class. Sums of lifts are lifts of sums, and their coboundaries add, proving additivity.

The map also does not depend on the finite-atlas path assignment. Compare a second family $\eta_x$ with $\gamma_x$, and first use the $\gamma$-normalized cocycle. Its evaluation on $\eta_x$ is $d(k_x)$, where $k_x=[\eta_x\overline\gamma_x]$. Thus its $\eta$-normalizing zero-cochain is $T_{\eta_x}^{\mathcal C}d(k_x)$. The explicit $\mathcal B$ zero-cochain $T_{\eta_x}^{\mathcal B}Q(k_x)$ lifts it, so subtracting its coboundary from $b$ produces a lift of the $\eta$ normalization with the same two-coboundary. Step 3.1 removes the initial change of representative. Coefficient morphisms commute with transport and the formulas, and images of chosen finite lifts are valid lifts for the image cocycle; independence of lifts therefore proves naturality. A commuting scalar action is treated by taking scalar multiples of lifts and using step 3.1.

If $[\alpha]$ comes from a $\mathcal B$ one-cocycle, normalize that cocycle using its own path evaluations. It lifts the normalized image cocycle and has zero coboundary, so its Bockstein is zero. Conversely if $\beta[\alpha]=0$, the lift $b$ from step 2.1 has $\delta b=i(\delta a_1)$ for some $\mathcal A$ one-cochain $a_1$. Then $b-i(a_1)$ is a $\mathcal B$ one-cocycle whose image is $\alpha^0$, so $[\alpha]$ is in the image of $q_*$. This proves exactness at $H^1(M;\mathcal C)$.

Every Bockstein two-cocycle becomes a coboundary in $\mathcal B$ by construction. Conversely let an $\mathcal A$ two-cocycle $a$ become a coboundary $i(a)=\delta b$ for one $\mathcal B$ one-cochain $b$. Its image $\alpha=q(b)$ is a $\mathcal C$ one-cocycle. The $\mathcal B$ zero-cochain $v_x=T_{\gamma_x}^{\mathcal B}b(\gamma_x)$, with $v_o=0$, lifts the normalizing zero-cochain for $\alpha$. Hence $b-\delta v$ lifts $\alpha^0$ and still has coboundary $i(a)$. By step 3.1 it computes the same Bockstein, so $\beta[\alpha]=[a]$. This proves exactness at $H^2(M;\mathcal A)$ and the asserted isomorphism when the two surrounding groups vanish. All lifts used either finitely many generator values, one base-fiber value, or a previously supplied whole cochain. No surjectivity of an infinite product of coefficient quotients was assumed.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.

The supplied collars give an open cover of $Y$ by a neighborhood of $W$ and a neighborhood of $X$, retracting onto $W,X$, with intersection retracting onto $A$. In collar coordinates this is obtained by adding a short collar segment across the seam to each side; shrinking its height linearly gives the three retractions. Hence [F1] gives the exact window
$$H_2(A;R)\xrightarrow{(i_W,-i_X)} H_2(W;R)\oplus H_2(X;R)\xrightarrow{j_W+j_X} H_2(Y;R)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_1(A;R) \xrightarrow{(i_W,-i_X)}H_1(W;R)\oplus H_1(X;R).$$
The last arrow is injective, since its $X$ coordinate is injective by hypothesis. Exactness therefore says that $j_W+j_X$ is surjective. This statement is elementwise and does not choose a simultaneous family of preimages.

Write $Q_Y=H_2(Y;R)/\operatorname{im}H_2(D\sqcup B;R)$ and let $\pi$ be its quotient map. Every $x\in H_2(X;R)$ is the image of a class in $H_2(B;R)$, by hypothesis. Its image in $H_2(Y;R)$ therefore lies in the boundary image, so $\pi j_X=0$. For any $y\in H_2(Y;R)$ choose, for this one $y$, a preimage $(w,x)$ under the surjection of step 1.1. Then $\pi(y)=\pi j_W(w)$. Thus $\pi j_W:H_2(W;R)\to Q_Y$ is surjective.

A class from $H_2(D;R)$ maps to zero under $\pi j_W$ because $D$ is a component union of $\partial Y$. A class $a\in H_2(A;R)$ has $j_Wi_W(a)=j_Xi_X(a)$ by the zero composite of the first two Mayer–Vietoris arrows. step 2.1 makes the latter class zero in $Q_Y$. Since $\partial W=A\sqcup D$, every boundary class of $W$ is a sum of these two kinds, so $\pi j_W$ vanishes on the full boundary image. It therefore factors uniquely through the displayed source quotient, and the factored map is surjective by step 2.1. This proves the claimed canonical map, without any assumption on $H_2(A;R)\to H_2(X;R)$.

If the source quotient is a vector space with a finite basis of size $r$, its $r$ images span the target. Finite elimination deletes linearly dependent images until a basis remains, so the target has dimension at most $r$. Only finitely many operations and selections occur. The proof also covers an empty seam or empty outer boundary, zero homology groups and the zero coefficient ring. No step selects representatives for infinitely many classes; surjectivity is used for a single class at a time. Thus the result and the finite-dimensional consequence require no choice principle.

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $M$ a right $R$-module, and $N$ a left $R$-module. Let

$$F:=\mathbb Z^{(M\times N)}$$

be the free $\mathbb Z$-module on the set $M\times N$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]], [[thm-universal-property-of-free-modules]]), and write $e_{(m,n)}$ for its standard basis elements. The additive group of $F$ is abelian. Let $H$ be the subgroup generated ([[def-generated-subgroup]]) by all elements

$$e_{(m+m',n)}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m',n)},$$

$$e_{(m,n+n')}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m,n')},$$

and

$$e_{(mr,n)}-e_{(m,rn)}$$

as $m,m'$ range over $M$, $n,n'$ over $N$, and $r$ over $R$. Since every subgroup of an abelian group is normal, the quotient group $F/H$ is defined ([[def-quotient-group]]). The **tensor product of $M$ and $N$ over $R$** is

$$M\otimes_RN:=F/H.$$

The coset of $e_{(m,n)}$ is the **elementary tensor** $m\otimes n$. Every tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors, because every element of $F$ is a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of basis elements and integer coefficients may be absorbed into either additive variable. The defining relations give

$$(m+m')\otimes n=m\otimes n+m'\otimes n,\qquad m\otimes(n+n')=m\otimes n+m\otimes n',$$

and

$$(mr)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn).$$

In particular $0\otimes n=0=m\otimes0$. No $R$-module structure on $M\otimes_RN$ is part of this arbitrary-ring definition; at this stage it is an abelian group.

Let $C_\bullet$ be a chain complex and let
$$\beta_n:B_n(C)\to Z_n(C)$$
be the canonical morphism supplied by
[[lem-the-boundary-subobject-factors-through-the-cycle-subobject]].

The **$n$th homology object** of $C$ is the cokernel
$$H_n(C):=\operatorname{coker}(\beta_n).$$

Equivalently, one writes
$$H_n(C)=Z_n(C)/B_n(C),$$
with the understanding that this quotient notation abbreviates the cokernel of
the canonical monomorphism from boundaries to cycles.

derivations.claim: For a finite set $S$ of left cosets $Hg$, let $B_S$ be the subgroup of $B$ consisting of sums supported on those cosets. It is a left $A$-submodule, and dropping all coefficients outside those cosets defines a left-$A$ linear projection $B\to B_S$ splitting inclusion. A finite choice of representatives $g_1,\ldots,g_r$ gives the explicit left-$A$ isomorphism $A^r\to B_S$, $(a_j)\mapsto\sum_j a_jg_j$: the supports of distinct summands are disjoint, and translating a supported sum by $g_j^{-1}$ proves surjectivity and uniqueness. Only representatives of this finite set of cosets are used; no global representative system is chosen. Every finite set of elements of $B$ lies in some such $B_S$, by taking the finitely many cosets that meet their supports.

For the fraction clause, send $as^{-1}\in F$, with $a,s\in A$ and $s\ne0$, to the same expression in $K$. If also $as^{-1}=bt^{-1}$ in $F$, choose a nonzero common right multiple $su=tv=w$ in $A$. Multiplying on the right by $w$ gives $au=bv$ in $A$, and the same identity in $K$ proves equality there. Thus the map is well-defined. At a common denominator the addition formula is $(au+bv)w^{-1}$ in both division rings. For a product $as^{-1}bt^{-1}$ with $b\ne0$, choose $bv=su$ nonzero in $A$. Then $s^{-1}b=uv^{-1}$ and the product is $au(tv)^{-1}$ in both rings; the case $b=0$ is immediate. Hence the map preserves multiplication, addition and unit. Its kernel is zero, since $as^{-1}=0$ implies $a=0$ in $K$ and hence in $A$. Uniqueness follows because a ring map extending $A$ must send the inverse of each nonzero $s\in A$ to its inverse in $K$.

Let $f:M'\to M$ be injective. A tensor $z\in M'\otimes_A B$ lies in the image of $M'\otimes_A B_S$ for a finite $S$, by [F1] and step 1.1. If $(f\otimes1)z=0$, apply $1\otimes(B\to B_S)$ to see that its representative $z_S$ maps to zero in $M\otimes_A B_S$. The explicit finite-free coordinates of step 1.1 identify this map with a finite direct sum of copies of $f$, so $z_S=0$ and $z=0$. For arbitrary maps $L\xrightarrow{f}M\xrightarrow{g}N$ exact at $M$, the same finite projection sends a tensor in $\ker(g\otimes1)$ into a finite direct sum of copies of $\ker g=\operatorname{im}f$. Lifting its finitely many coordinates gives a tensor in the image of $f\otimes1$. Conversely that image lies in the kernel since $gf=0$. A surjective map also remains surjective, by lifting the finitely many first coordinates of a tensor expression. Thus extension is exact for arbitrary right modules.

Dropping all coefficients outside $H$ defines an $A$-bimodule map $p:B\to A$ with $p(1)=1$: multiplication by a group element of $H$ on either side preserves both $H$ and its complement. Balancing therefore defines $\rho_M:M\otimes_A B\to M$, $\rho_M(m\otimes b)=mp(b)$. It is right-$A$ linear and satisfies $\rho_M(m\otimes1)=m$. This proves the split unit assertion. If $f\otimes1=0$ for a module homomorphism $f$, then $f(m)=\rho_N((f\otimes1)(m\otimes1))=0$ for each $m$; the functor is faithful. Apply step 2.1 to the exact sequences defining cycles, boundaries and their quotient. It identifies tensor cycles with the kernel of the tensor differential, tensor boundaries with its image, and the tensor quotient with their quotient. The resulting map is $[z]\otimes b\mapsto[z\otimes b]$, proving the natural homology assertion degree by degree. Replacing left cosets by right cosets gives the same finite-coordinate proof for left modules, and the same coefficient projection splits their unit map.

Suppose $q\in F\cap B$. Write $q=as^{-1}$ with $a,s\in A$, $s\ne0$, so $qs=a$. Partition the finite support of $q$ into right cosets $gH$ and choose finitely many representatives, using $1$ for the coset $H$ if it occurs. Thus $q=\sum_j g_jq_j$ with $q_j\in A$. Right multiplication by $s$ preserves each of these coset supports. Since $a$ is supported on $H$, every summand outside that coset satisfies $g_jq_js=0$ as a group-ring element. The absence of zero divisors in $B$ and $s\ne0$ imply $q_j=0$ for each such summand. Therefore $q$ is supported on $H$, which means $q\in A$. The reverse inclusion is given, so $F\cap B=A$. The map of additive quotients $F/A\to K/B$ is well-defined, has kernel $(F\cap B)/A=0$, and respects both $A$ actions because all inclusions are ring maps. Every representative, denominator, lift and coordinate set in this proof belongs to a single finite argument; no simultaneous infinite family is selected. This proves all assertions without a choice principle.
