Let $L$ be a finite geometric simplicial complex with an ordered vertex set, and let $\mathcal R$ be a local system of rank-one free right modules over an arbitrary unital ring $R$. Its finite simplicial chain complex $F_*(L;\mathcal R)$ and intrinsic singular chain complex $C_*(L;\mathcal R)$ admit $R$-linear chain maps
$$P:C_*(L;\mathcal R)\to F_*(L;\mathcal R),\qquad J:F_*(L;\mathcal R)\to C_*(L;\mathcal R)$$
with $PJ=1$ and an explicitly constructed chain homotopy $JP\simeq1$. Choices of bases at its finitely many vertices make $F_*$ bounded finite-free.

Consequently, for every compact connected Hausdorff topological manifold $M$, with boundary allowed, and every such local system supplied with a base-fiber identification with $R$, its nonnegative singular chain complex is free with a formula-specified basis and is $R$-linearly chain-homotopy dominated by a bounded finite-free complex. No choice principle, triangulation of $M$, or assertion of finite CW type for $M$ is assumed.

Work in ZF. Let $A$ be any associative unital ring and let $C$ be a chain complex of unital right $A$-modules with $C_n=0$ for $n<0$. Supply a chain complex $F$ with $F_n=0$ outside $0\le n\le m$, each $F_n$ supplied as a finite free right $A$-module, chain maps $f:C\to F$ and $g:F\to C$, and right $A$-linear maps $h_n:C_n\to C_{n+1}$ such that
$$1_C-gf=d_Ch+hd_C.$$
Then there is a chain complex $E$ of finitely generated projective right $A$-modules, zero outside $0\le n\le N$ for some finite $N$, together with explicitly constructed chain maps $a:C\to E$, $b:E\to C$ and chain homotopies
$$1_C-ba=dH+Hd,\qquad 1_E-ab=dL+Ld.$$
The modules of $E$ below its top degree can be taken finite free, and its top module is the image of an explicit idempotent on $\bigoplus_{j=0}^mF_j$.

Neither freeness nor projectivity nor finite generation of the modules of $C$ is required. Thus the result applies in particular to the nonnegative singular or cellular free chain complexes with specified bases. More generally it applies after reindexing whenever $C$ and $F$ have a common finite lower bound. It makes no assertion for inputs unbounded below and no assertion that $E$ is finite free or that any underlying space has finite CW type. No form of the Axiom of Choice is assumed.

Let $k$ be a commutative field, let $G$ be PTFA, put $A=k[G]$, and supply its Ore fraction division ring $K$. Subscripts $k$ and $K$ mean tensor base change along augmentation $A\to k$ and inclusion $A\to K$, respectively.

For every finitely generated projective right-$A$ module $P$,
$$\dim_K P_K=\dim_k P_k<\infty.$$
For a homomorphism $f:P\to Q$ between such modules,
$$\dim_K\operatorname{im}f_K\ge\dim_k\operatorname{im}f_k.$$
Consequently, for any bounded complex $P_*$ of finitely generated projective right-$A$ modules,
$$\sum_i(-1)^i\dim_K H_i(P_K)=\sum_i(-1)^i\dim_k H_i(P_k).$$
If additionally the complex is nonnegative, $\dim_k H_0(P_k)=1$ and $H_0(P_K)=0$, then
$$\dim_K H_1(P_K)\le\dim_k H_1(P_k)-1.$$
No choice principle or free basis for a projective module is assumed.

Thus its two models have the actual $k$ and $K$ homology of $N$. By [F2] and step 1.1, $\dim_K H_1(N;K)\le1-1=0$, so it is zero. Let $P\cup\eta$ be a smooth oriented two-component link in $S^3$ with unknotted axis $\eta$, and let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot. Supply disjoint closed product tubes and positive meridian/preferred zero-linking-longitude peripheral data for the knots and axis. Write $P(K)$ for infection along $\eta$ with the untwisted companion $K$. For a knot $L$, write $M(L)$ for its actual chosen zero-longitude filling, with the orientation extending its exterior. Let $w=\operatorname{lk}(P,\eta)$.

There is a compact oriented smooth cobordism $E$ with
$$\partial E=M(P)\sqcup M(K)\sqcup(-M(P(K))).$$
For any commutative unital coefficient ring $R$, it has $H_1(E;R)=R$ and $H_2(E;R)=R^2$. The two first boundary components induce the displayed basis in degree two. If $s_L=\alpha_L\cap[M(L)]$ where $\alpha_L\in H^1(M(L);R)$ evaluates as $1$ on the positive meridian, then, in those coordinates,
$$i_*s_{P(K)}=i_*s_P+w\,i_*s_K.$$
In degree one the meridians of $P$, $K$ and $P(K)$ map to $1,w,1$, respectively.

Likewise, for any finite nonempty list of knots $K_1,\ldots,K_q$ with the same supplied peripheral data, there is a compact oriented smooth cobordism $C$ from $\bigsqcup_j M(K_j)$ to $M(K_1\#\cdots\#K_q)$, with $H_1(C;R)=R$ and $H_2(C;R)=R^q$. The incoming degree-two classes are its coordinate basis and the outgoing class maps to their sum. In particular, for $X=E$ or $C$, the outgoing inclusions are injective on $H_1,H_2$ and the union of incoming components surjects onto $H_2(X;R)$.

The peripheral and framing data are supplied, rather than selected by an existence theorem. Their subsequent construction and the homology assertions use no additional choice principle. This is an ordinary-coefficient assertion; arbitrary twisted-coefficient boundary generation is not asserted.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring. Let $W$ and $X$ be compact manifolds with supplied boundary collars and decompositions $\partial W=A\sqcup D$ and $\partial X=A\sqcup B$, where each summand is a union of boundary components. Glue the two copies of $A$ by a supplied homeomorphism, obtaining $Y=W\cup_A X$ with $\partial Y=D\sqcup B$. All homology below has constant coefficients $R$. Suppose
$$H_1(A;R)\longrightarrow H_1(X;R)\ \text{is injective},\qquad H_2(B;R)\longrightarrow H_2(X;R)\ \text{is surjective}.$$
Then inclusion of $W$ induces a well-defined surjection
$$\frac{H_2(W;R)}{\operatorname{im}H_2(\partial W;R)} \twoheadrightarrow \frac{H_2(Y;R)}{\operatorname{im}H_2(\partial Y;R)}.$$
In particular, if $R$ is a field and the first quotient is finite dimensional, the dimension of the second quotient is at most that of the first. No injectivity assumption on $H_2(A;R)\to H_2(X;R)$, orientability, or choice principle is needed.

Let $W,X$ be compact oriented topological four-manifolds with supplied boundary collars and decompositions $\partial W=A\sqcup D$, $\partial X=A\sqcup B$. Glue their copies of $A$ by a supplied orientation-reversing identification, obtaining $Y=W\cup_A X$ with $\partial Y=D\sqcup B$. Supply one ambient rank-one right-$R$ local system on $Y$, where $R$ is an involutive unital ring. On each connected component supply a base-fiber identification with $R$ and unitary monodromy, and use its transported standard Hermitian form. Use its restrictions and the induced orientations on $W,X$.

For the intersection pairings defined by inverse relative cap duality, passage to absolute cohomology and evaluation,
$$\lambda_Y(i_*p,i_*q)=\lambda_W(p,q)\qquad(p,q\in H_2(W;R)).$$
In particular all isotropic and dual-pair identities for homology classes in $W$ persist under their inclusion in $Y$. The result applies to topological manifolds and requires no geometric surface transversality or choice principle.

Let $W$ be a compact connected oriented topological four-manifold with supplied boundary collar, and let $R$ be an involutive unital ring. Supply a based rank-one right-$R$ local system $\mathcal R$, a base-fiber identification with $R$, unitary monodromy and its parallel standard Hermitian form. For $p\in H_2(W;\mathcal R)$ let $a_p\in H^2(W,\partial W;\mathcal R^\vee)$ be the inverse cap-duality image of $\bar p$, using the form to identify the intrinsic dual system with $\overline{\mathcal R}$. Define
$$\lambda(p,q)=\langle j(a_p),q\rangle,$$
where $j$ forgets the relative condition and the last pairing is intrinsic cochain evaluation. Then
$$\lambda(p,q)=\overline{\lambda(q,p)}$$
for all $p,q$. In particular $\lambda(\ell_i,d_j)=\delta_{ij}$ implies $\lambda(d_j,\ell_i)=\delta_{ij}$. No choice axiom, triangulation or geometric transversality of surfaces in dimension four is required.

Let $W$ be a compact connected oriented Hausdorff topological four-manifold and put $M=\partial W$, allowing $M$ empty. Let $k$ be a commutative field, $G$ a PTFA group, and $\phi:\pi_1(W)\to G$ a supplied coefficient homomorphism. Write $K$ for the fraction division ring of $k[G]$, with its standard involution, and use the induced rank-one right-coefficient systems. Suppose $\dim_kH_1(M_j;k)=1$ for each connected component $M_j$ of $M$. Then
$$\dim_K\operatorname{coker}\{H_2(M;K)\to H_2(W;K)\}\le\dim_k\operatorname{coker}\{H_2(M;k)\to H_2(W;k)\}.$$
All dimensions in the formula are finite. No choice axiom, smoothness, triangulation, or supplied finite CW model of $W$ is assumed.

Let $N$ be a compact connected Hausdorff topological manifold, with boundary allowed, and let $k$ be a commutative field with $\dim_k H_1(N;k)=1$. Let $\phi:\pi_1(N)\to G$ be nontrivial with $G$ PTFA, and let $K$ be the Ore fraction division ring of $k[G]$. Then $H_0(N;K)=H_1(N;K)=0$. No choice principle or finite CW model for $N$ is assumed.

Let $W$ be a compact connected oriented topological four-manifold with a supplied boundary collar, and put $M=\partial W$. Let $R\subseteq K$ be a unital involution-stable subring of an involutive division ring. Supply a based rank-one right-$R$ coefficient system $\mathcal R$ on $W$, with its base fiber identified with $R$, unitary monodromy and the transported standard Hermitian form. Write $H_*(W;R)$ and $H_*(W;K)$ for its homology and scalar-extended homology.

Define the equivariant intersection pairing $\lambda_R$ by sending $\bar p\in\overline{H_2(W;R)}$ through inverse relative cap duality to $H^2(W,M;\mathcal R^\vee)$, then into $H^2(W;\mathcal R^\vee)$, then evaluating on $q\in H_2(W;R)$. Here $\mathcal R^\vee$ is the intrinsic dual coefficient system, identified with the conjugate system by the supplied Hermitian form. Thus $\lambda_R(p,q)$ is conjugate-linear in $p$ and right-linear in $q$. Define $\lambda_K$ by the same construction over $K$.

Suppose $m\ge0$ and classes $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_m,d_1,\ldots,d_m\in H_2(W;R)$ satisfy
$$\lambda_R(\ell_i,\ell_j)=0,\qquad\lambda_R(\ell_i,d_j)=\lambda_R(d_j,\ell_i)=\delta_{ij},$$
and suppose
$$\dim_K\bigl(H_2(W;K)/\operatorname{im}H_2(M;K)\bigr)\le2m.$$
Let $M_0$ be one connected boundary component with $H_1(M_0;K)=0$. Its coefficient Bockstein, oriented cap duality and evaluation define the linking form $B_0$ with values in $K/R$. Then
$$B_0(x,y)=0\quad\text{for all }x,y\in\ker\{H_1(M_0;R)\longrightarrow H_1(W;R)\}.$$
No vanishing condition on the other boundary components is imposed. No choice axiom, finite CW structure, or general noncommutative universal-coefficient theorem is assumed.

Let $W$ be a compact oriented Hausdorff topological $n$-manifold with boundary $A$ and a supplied boundary collar $c:A\times[0,1)\to W$. Let $\mathcal L$ be a local system of abelian groups. Cap with the integral relative orientation class $z=[W,A]$ gives isomorphisms in every integer degree:
$$H^p(W,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(W;\mathcal L),\qquad H^p(W;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(W,A;\mathcal L).$$
The maps commute with every coefficient action commuting with transport, including noncommutative ring actions on the underlying abelian-group systems. No choice principle, smoothness, triangulation or finite CW structure is assumed.

Let $R$ be a unital ring with $1\ne0$ and no zero divisors. Suppose both Ore conditions hold: any two nonzero elements have a nonzero common right multiple and a nonzero common left multiple. Let $R\subseteq K$ be a unital embedding into a division ring such that every element of $K$ is a right fraction $as^{-1}$ with $a\in R$ and $0\ne s\in R$.

For every right $R$-module $M$, the right $K$-module $M\otimes_RK$ is represented by fractions $[m,s]$ with $m\in M$ and $0\ne s\in R$, corresponding to $m\otimes s^{-1}$. The equality criterion is
$$[m,s]=[n,t]\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{there exist }0\ne u,v\in R\text{ with }su=tv\text{ and }mu=nv.$$
In particular, $[m,s]=0$ if and only if $ma=0$ for some $0\ne a\in R$. Thus the kernel of $M\to M\otimes_RK$, $m\mapsto m\otimes1$, is exactly the set of elements with a nonzero right annihilator, and $M\otimes_RK=0$ if and only if every element of $M$ has a nonzero right annihilator.

The functor $-\otimes_RK$ is exact on arbitrary right $R$-modules, so $K$ is flat as a left $R$-module. For every chain complex $C_\bullet$ of right $R$-modules, the canonical map gives a natural isomorphism
$$H_i(C_\bullet)\otimes_RK\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }H_i(C_\bullet\otimes_RK)$$
for every integer $i$. No finite-generation, finite-presentation or boundedness assumption on the modules or complexes is required.

The corresponding left-module assertions also hold: $K$ is flat as a right $R$-module, $1\otimes m$ is zero in $K\otimes_RM$ precisely when $am=0$ for some $0\ne a\in R$, and $K\otimes_R-$ commutes with the homology of arbitrary left-module chain complexes. All assertions require no choice axiom.

If $M$ is a compact topological manifold with boundary $A=\partial M$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $A$ and a homeomorphism
$$c:A\times[0,1)\xrightarrow{\sim}V,\qquad c(x,0)=x.$$
Consequently $A\hookrightarrow M$ is an unbased cofibration, and $M\setminus A\hookrightarrow M$ is a homotopy equivalence. The manifold is Hausdorff and second countable by convention. All three conclusions require no AC.

derivations.claim: The factorization supplies an involution-preserving ring homomorphism $\mathbb Z[\Pi_s]\to A$, and hence maps of all actual coefficient chain systems on $V$. Cap, dual-system identification and evaluation commute with this change of coefficients. Explicitly a dual cochain $f$ changes to $c\otimes a\mapsto\rho(f(c))a$; balancing and the finite face formulas show compatibility with coboundaries and cap. Both relative cap maps are isomorphisms by [F5], so their inverse duality maps commute too. Thus the image classes on $V$ retain the displayed zero and unit pairings. The standard base vector $1$ gives compatible transported Hermitian structures before and after change of ring. Hermitian symmetry [F2] supplies the reverse cross-pairing $\lambda_A(d_j,\ell_i)=\delta_{ij}$.

The ordinary group $H_2(V;k)$ has dimension $2r$. For $k=\mathbb Q$ this is exact rational localization of the integral singular complex, using [F5]. For $k=\mathbb F_p$ one can check the coefficient sequence directly without an infinite lifting assertion. Lift the finitely many coefficients of an $\mathbb F_p$ two-cycle $z$ to an integral chain $\widetilde z$. Write $\partial\widetilde z=pw$; then $w$ is an integral one-cycle and $p[w]=0$. Since $H_1(V;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$, $w=\partial v$ for some two-chain $v$, so $\widetilde z-pv$ is an integral cycle lifting $z$. Conversely, if an integral two-cycle becomes a boundary mod $p$, lift that one finite bounding three-chain and subtract its boundary; the difference is $p$ times an integral two-cycle, since integral chain groups have no $p$-torsion. Thus $H_2(V;\mathbb F_p)\cong H_2(V;\mathbb Z)/p=\mathbb F_p^{2r}$. Its quotient by the boundary image therefore has dimension at most $2r$.

Give $V$ its collar from [F5] and use the actual product collars of the finite standard pieces. At each attachment the outgoing $H_1$ injection and incoming $H_2$ surjection of [F1] give a surjection from the preceding boundary cokernel to the new one. Its dimension cannot increase, so after finitely many attachments the ordinary cokernel is at most $2r$. The single coefficient system on final $W$ restricts to each intermediate manifold, and [F2] preserves every pair identity under inclusion. Thus the images $\ell_i,d_i$ in final $W$ satisfy all pair identities in the Statement. Orientation reversal of a piece does not change its ordinary injection and surjection properties; the orientation on the embedded preceding manifold is unchanged, which is the orientation used in [F2]. All the resulting manifolds are compact and oriented with the actual remaining boundary components.

Every remaining boundary component is a chosen zero-longitude surgery on a knot. Its ordinary first homology over $k$ is $k$: in the exterior/filling Mayer–Vietoris sequence the preferred longitude maps to zero, the filling core identifies with the meridian, and that meridian remains the single free generator, exactly as in the peripheral calculation of [F1]. Hence [F3] applies to final $W$ and gives the first cokernel inequality in the Statement. If the restriction to $M_0$ is nontrivial, the second assertion of [F3] gives $H_1(M_0;K)=0$. Thus the finite pairs of step 2.1 and the localized dimension bound verify every hypothesis of [F4], with $R=A$ and the standard involutive fraction ring $K$.

Apply [F4] to obtain $B_0(a,b)=0$ for all classes in that inclusion kernel. If $B_0(a,a)\ne0$, the class $a$ therefore cannot lie in the kernel, and its image in $H_1(W;A)$ is nonzero. This is the survival implication used for infection axes in the source bordism argument. Every isotropic submodule has zero self-pairings, so such a surviving class lies outside every isotropic submodule.

For actual integral $s$-solution data, these hypotheses are precisely its homology and lifted-pairing part; passage to a quotient target of derived length at most $s$ factors because a homomorphism carries the ordinary derived series into the target derived series. Every coefficient lift in step 1.2 involved one finite chain; all other arguments used the supplied finite pair list and actual collared attachments. The proof therefore preserves smooth and topological scopes and introduces no choice axiom beyond none in these data.

Let $W$ be a compact oriented Hausdorff topological $n$-manifold with boundary $A$ and a supplied boundary collar $c:A\times[0,1)\to W$. Let $\mathcal L$ be a local system of abelian groups. Cap with the integral relative orientation class $z=[W,A]$ gives isomorphisms in every integer degree:
$$H^p(W,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(W;\mathcal L),\qquad H^p(W;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(W,A;\mathcal L).$$
The maps commute with every coefficient action commuting with transport, including noncommutative ring actions on the underlying abelian-group systems. No choice principle, smoothness, triangulation or finite CW structure is assumed.

Let $M$ be a compact oriented boundaryless Hausdorff topological $n$-manifold and let $\mathcal L$ be a local system of abelian groups. Cap with its integral orientation class induces isomorphisms
$$H^p(M;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;\mathcal L)$$
for every integer $p$, without a choice principle. The maps respect any coefficient-ring action commuting with transport, and in particular apply to local systems of modules over a noncommutative ring by forgetting to abelian groups and retaining that action. No smoothness, triangulation or prescribed finite CW structure is assumed.

Let $(M,o)$ be a compact connected based Hausdorff manifold, let $R$ be an involutive unital ring, and supply a rank-one right-$R$ local system $\mathcal R$ with an identification $\mathcal R_o=R$. Assume every based-loop monodromy is left multiplication by a unit $u$ satisfying $\bar u=u^{-1}$. Equip the base fiber with the standard Hermitian form $h_o(a,b)=\bar a b$. Transport extends this to a path-independent parallel Hermitian form $h$ on $\mathcal R$. Put $C_*=C_*(M;\mathcal R)$. For a right $R$-module $P$, write $\overline P$ for its conjugate left module, with $r\cdot\bar p=\overline{p\bar r}$.

The left-$R$ cochain complex $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R)$ is the intrinsic cochain complex of the left-$R$ local system with fiber $R$ and transport $a\mapsto au^{-1}$. Relative to the supplied parallel Hermitian form, that local system is naturally isomorphic to $\overline{\mathcal R}$ by $\bar v\mapsto[w\mapsto h(v,w)]$. The identifications are independent of unitary fiber frames; an arbitrary change of Hermitian structure is not asserted to preserve them. If $M$ is oriented, boundaryless and of dimension $n$, cap duality therefore gives
$$H^p(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R))\cong\overline{H_{n-p}(C_*)}.$$
If $R\subseteq K$ is an embedding into an involutive division ring extending the involution, the same conclusion is valid for $K$, with $C_*\otimes_R K$ in the homology target. If $R$ is involution-stable in $K$, the complex $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,K/R)$ is the corresponding intrinsic left-$R$ cochain complex with fiber $K/R$ and transport by right multiplication by $u^{-1}$. These identifications require no choice principle and commute with the coefficient maps $R\to K\to K/R$.

Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff manifold, $o\in M$, and $R$ a unital ring. One can construct paths $\gamma_x$ from $o$ to every $x\in M$, with $\gamma_o$ constant, by fixed rules from one finite atlas and finitely many connecting paths. Let $\mathcal R$ be a right-$R$ local system with a supplied identification $\mathcal R_o=R$ and transport given by left multiplication by units, with monodromy image $H\le R^\times$. Its twisted singular complex has an explicit chain decomposition $C_*(M;\mathcal R)=C'_*\oplus Q_*$ after a change of free bases, where $C'_0=R$, $C'_* $ is free, and $Q_*$ is contractible with its only nonzero differential an identity from degree one to degree zero. Moreover
$$\operatorname{im}(d'_1)=\sum_{h\in H}(h-1)R.$$
The decomposition and its dual cochain homotopy equivalences require no choice principle. In particular this image is principal if $H$ is cyclic, if it equals $R$, or if every right ideal of $R$ is principal.

Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff manifold with a basepoint, and let $0\to\mathcal A\xrightarrow{i}\mathcal B\xrightarrow{q}\mathcal C\to0$ be a short exact sequence of local systems of abelian groups on $M$. There is a natural coefficient Bockstein making the sequence
$$H^1(M;\mathcal B)\xrightarrow{q_*}H^1(M;\mathcal C)\xrightarrow{\beta}H^2(M;\mathcal A)\xrightarrow{i_*}H^2(M;\mathcal B)$$
exact at its two middle terms. In particular $\beta$ is an isomorphism if $H^1(M;\mathcal B)=H^2(M;\mathcal B)=0$. No choice principle is assumed. If the local systems and maps have a commuting coefficient-ring action, the sequence and Bockstein respect it.

For $A\subseteq X$ and a local system $\mathcal L$ on $X$, restriction to $A$ gives natural exact sequences
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;\mathcal L|_A)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\partial}H_{n-1}(A;\mathcal L|_A)\to\cdots$$
and
$$\cdots\to H^n(X,A;\mathcal L)\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(A;\mathcal L|_A)\xrightarrow{\delta}H^{n+1}(X,A;\mathcal L)\to\cdots.$$
The homology connector sends a relative cycle represented by $c$ to $[\partial c]$. The cohomology connector sends a cocycle $a$ on $A$ to $[\delta\widetilde a]$, where $\widetilde a$ is its extension by zero to simplices not contained in $A$. Naturality uses the variances of the preceding functoriality proposition.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring and let $\mathcal L,\mathcal K$ be left $R$-module local systems on $X$. Their **objectwise tensor product** is
$$(\mathcal L\otimes_R\mathcal K)_x=\mathcal L_x\otimes_R\mathcal K_x,\qquad T_\gamma(\ell\otimes k)=T_\gamma\ell\otimes T_\gamma k.$$
The tensor relations make the displayed transport well defined; identity and composition hold on elementary tensors, and $T_{\bar\gamma}\otimes T_{\bar\gamma}$ is its inverse. Thus this is again a local system.

A **local-coefficient pairing** is a natural transformation $b:\mathcal L\otimes_R\mathcal K\to\mathcal N$, equivalently bilinear maps $b_x:\mathcal L_x\times\mathcal K_x\to\mathcal N_x$ satisfying $T_\gamma b_x(\ell,k)=b_y(T_\gamma\ell,T_\gamma k)$ for every path class $\gamma:x\to y$.

For a simplex $\sigma:[v_0,\ldots,v_{p+q}]\to X$, let $\lambda_{0p}^\sigma$ be its affine edge path from $v_0$ to $v_p$. For $\varphi\in C^p(X;\mathcal L)$ and $\psi\in C^q(X;\mathcal K)$ define
$$(\varphi\smile_b\psi)(\sigma)=b_{v_0}\left(\varphi(\sigma[0,\ldots,p]),T^{\mathcal K}_{\overline{\lambda_{0p}^\sigma}}\psi(\sigma[p,\ldots,p+q])\right).$$
The reverse transport is necessary because the back-face value lies over $v_p$ while the output cochain value must lie over $v_0$. The Alexander--Whitney face calculation, with naturality of $b$ on each triangular transport comparison, gives
$$\delta(\varphi\smile_b\psi)=\delta\varphi\smile_b\psi+(-1)^p\varphi\smile_b\delta\psi.$$
Hence cocycles give cup products in cohomology. The same vanishing-on-front-face argument as for ordinary relative cups gives $H^p(X,A;\mathcal L)\otimes_RH^q(X,B;\mathcal K)\to H^{p+q}(X,A\cup B;\mathcal N)$ under the usual excisive-triad comparison.

For $\varphi\in C^p(X;\mathcal L)$ and a local chain generator $m\sigma\in C_n(X;\mathcal K)$, define the **cohomology-first cap product** by zero when $p>n$ and otherwise by
$$\varphi\cap_b(m\sigma)=T^{\mathcal N}_{\lambda_{0p}^\sigma}\left(b_{v_0}(\varphi(\sigma[0,\ldots,p]),m)\right)\sigma[p,\ldots,n].$$
Here forward transport is necessary because the retained back face begins at $v_p$. The published front/back face cancellation, with the same naturality squares, yields
$$\partial(\varphi\cap_b c)=(-1)^p\left(\varphi\cap_b\partial c-\delta\varphi\cap_b c\right).$$
Consequently cap descends to the same relative quotient patterns as [[def-relative-cap-product]], with the chain coefficient system changed from $\mathcal K$ to $\mathcal N$ in the target. In particular,
$$H^p(X,A;\mathcal L)\otimes_RH_n(X,A;\mathcal K)\longrightarrow H_{n-p}(X;\mathcal N),$$
and
$$H^p(X;\mathcal L)\otimes_RH_n(X,A;\mathcal K)\longrightarrow H_{n-p}(X,A;\mathcal N).$$

If a cohomology class is represented with compact support $K$, cup with any ordinary class remains supported in $K$, while the cap of a class in $H^p(X,X\setminus K;\mathcal L)$ with a class in $H_n(X,X\setminus K;\mathcal K)$ is an absolute class. Enlargement of $K$ commutes with the formulas, giving the compact-support cup and supportwise cap operations used in duality. Constant systems and multiplication recover the published operations. Empty spaces, zero systems or rings, $p=0$, $p=n$, and $p>n$ follow from the displayed formulas. Only finite faces of a supplied simplex occur, so no AC is used.

derivations.claim: Write $M=\partial W$. Under relative cap duality, the map $j:H^2(W,M;K^\vee)\to H^2(W;K^\vee)$ corresponds to the intersection map on $H_2(W;K)$. This map is zero under the given boundary-generation hypothesis. Indeed, if $z=i_*b$ for $b\in H_2(M;K)$, closed duality represents $\bar b$ by a degree-one cohomology class on $M$. Its pair connector is the relative dual class of $\bar z$, by the cap boundary identity, and its image under $j$ is zero by exactness. Every $z$ has this form by hypothesis. Thus $j=0$, with intrinsic dual systems identified using the supplied Hermitian form.

Extend $x$ by zero from $N$ to $H_1(M;R)$. Since it dies in $W$, the pair sequence supplies $a\in H_2(W,M;R)$ with $\partial a=x$. Absolute cap duality sends its conjugate to $u\in H^2(W;R^\vee)$, whose boundary restriction is the dual of $\bar x$, by the signed cap boundary formula in degree two. The image of $x$ in $H_1(M;K)$ is zero: on selected components this is the assumed vanishing and on other components $x$ was zero. Hence $u_K|_M=0$. Pair exactness puts $u_K$ in the image of $j$, which is zero by step 1.1. Choose one $R^\vee$-valued two-cocycle representing $u$. Since its image represents zero over $K$, one whole $K^\vee$-valued one-cochain $b$ satisfies $\delta b=u$. Its quotient $\nu=b\bmod R$ is a $(K/R)^\vee$-valued cocycle on $W$, and on each selected component its coefficient Bockstein is the dual of $\bar x$. This constructs a whole cochain, rather than choosing lifts of infinitely many quotient coefficients.

On a selected connected component $N_j$, closed duality gives $H^2(N_j;K^\vee)=0$ from $H_1(N_j;K)=0$. Also $H^1(N_j;K^\vee)=0$. To see this without a universal-coefficient theorem, use the one-vertex model over $K$ from [F3], so $C_0=K$. Its $d_1$ image is either zero or $K$. In the first case $H_1=0$ says $C_1=\operatorname{im}d_2$, so every one-cocycle vanishes. In the second case one vector $v$ with $d_1v=1$ splits $C_1=\ker d_1\oplus vK$; a one-cocycle vanishes on $\ker d_1=\operatorname{im}d_2$, so equals a zero-cochain composed with $d_1$. The dual identification in [F2] preserves these assertions. Exactness [F3] therefore makes the degree-one coefficient Bockstein an isomorphism. Consequently the restriction of $[\nu]$ in step 2.1 is exactly the inverse-Bockstein class defining the linking form of $x|_{N_j}$. This applies to the finite component list separately.

Let $y$ also belong to the displayed kernel. Its image cycle in $W$ is the boundary of a single $R$-valued two-chain $c$. The sum of the component linking evaluations is therefore $
u(y)=
u(\partial c)=\delta
u(c)=0$. Different components do not have cross terms because the chain and cochain groups on the finite disjoint union split componentwise; their cap fundamental classes carry their induced orientations. This is precisely $B_N(x,y)$. The proof used only finite component operations, exactness and one individual cochain witness, and made no assertion about the other boundary components.

Let $P\cup\eta$ be a smooth oriented two-component link in $S^3$ with unknotted axis $\eta$, and let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot. Supply disjoint closed product tubes and positive meridian/preferred zero-linking-longitude peripheral data for the knots and axis. Write $P(K)$ for infection along $\eta$ with the untwisted companion $K$. For a knot $L$, write $M(L)$ for its actual chosen zero-longitude filling, with the orientation extending its exterior. Let $w=\operatorname{lk}(P,\eta)$.

There is a compact oriented smooth cobordism $E$ with
$$\partial E=M(P)\sqcup M(K)\sqcup(-M(P(K))).$$
For any commutative unital coefficient ring $R$, it has $H_1(E;R)=R$ and $H_2(E;R)=R^2$. The two first boundary components induce the displayed basis in degree two. If $s_L=\alpha_L\cap[M(L)]$ where $\alpha_L\in H^1(M(L);R)$ evaluates as $1$ on the positive meridian, then, in those coordinates,
$$i_*s_{P(K)}=i_*s_P+w\,i_*s_K.$$
In degree one the meridians of $P$, $K$ and $P(K)$ map to $1,w,1$, respectively.

Likewise, for any finite nonempty list of knots $K_1,\ldots,K_q$ with the same supplied peripheral data, there is a compact oriented smooth cobordism $C$ from $\bigsqcup_j M(K_j)$ to $M(K_1\#\cdots\#K_q)$, with $H_1(C;R)=R$ and $H_2(C;R)=R^q$. The incoming degree-two classes are its coordinate basis and the outgoing class maps to their sum. In particular, for $X=E$ or $C$, the outgoing inclusions are injective on $H_1,H_2$ and the union of incoming components surjects onto $H_2(X;R)$.

The peripheral and framing data are supplied, rather than selected by an existence theorem. Their subsequent construction and the homology assertions use no additional choice principle. This is an ordinary-coefficient assertion; arbitrary twisted-coefficient boundary generation is not asserted.

Let $W$ be a compact connected oriented Hausdorff topological four-manifold and put $M=\partial W$, allowing $M$ empty. Let $k$ be a commutative field, $G$ a PTFA group, and $\phi:\pi_1(W)\to G$ a supplied coefficient homomorphism. Write $K$ for the fraction division ring of $k[G]$, with its standard involution, and use the induced rank-one right-coefficient systems. Suppose $\dim_kH_1(M_j;k)=1$ for each connected component $M_j$ of $M$. Then
$$\dim_K\operatorname{coker}\{H_2(M;K)\to H_2(W;K)\}\le\dim_k\operatorname{coker}\{H_2(M;k)\to H_2(W;k)\}.$$
All dimensions in the formula are finite. No choice axiom, smoothness, triangulation, or supplied finite CW model of $W$ is assumed.

Let $N$ be a compact connected Hausdorff topological manifold, with boundary allowed, and let $k$ be a commutative field with $\dim_k H_1(N;k)=1$. Let $\phi:\pi_1(N)\to G$ be nontrivial with $G$ PTFA, and let $K$ be the Ore fraction division ring of $k[G]$. Then $H_0(N;K)=H_1(N;K)=0$. No choice principle or finite CW model for $N$ is assumed.

Let $W$ be a compact connected oriented topological four-manifold with a supplied boundary collar. Supply a unital involution-stable inclusion $R\subseteq K$ into an involutive division ring and a based rank-one right-$R$ coefficient system on $W$, with unitary monodromy and the transported standard Hermitian form. Suppose
$$H_2(W;K)=\operatorname{im}\{H_2(\partial W;K)\longrightarrow H_2(W;K)\}.$$
Let $N$ be a finite union of connected boundary components, each satisfying $H_1(N_j;K)=0$, with its induced boundary orientation and coefficient system. On each component define the linking form by inverse coefficient Bockstein, inverse oriented cap duality and evaluation; let $B_N$ be their orthogonal sum. Then
$$B_N(x,y)=0\quad\text{whenever }x,y\in\ker\{H_1(N;R)\longrightarrow H_1(W;R)\}.$$
No choice axiom or finite CW structure is assumed. No vanishing condition is imposed on the unselected boundary components.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.

For $A\subseteq X$ and a local system $\mathcal L$ on $X$, restriction to $A$ gives natural exact sequences
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;\mathcal L|_A)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\partial}H_{n-1}(A;\mathcal L|_A)\to\cdots$$
and
$$\cdots\to H^n(X,A;\mathcal L)\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(A;\mathcal L|_A)\xrightarrow{\delta}H^{n+1}(X,A;\mathcal L)\to\cdots.$$
The homology connector sends a relative cycle represented by $c$ to $[\partial c]$. The cohomology connector sends a cocycle $a$ on $A$ to $[\delta\widetilde a]$, where $\widetilde a$ is its extension by zero to simplices not contained in $A$. Naturality uses the variances of the preceding functoriality proposition.

derivations.claim: Use the actual product gluing from [F1]. Put $S=N(\eta)=V_K$, $T_0=\partial S$, $A=M(P)\setminus\operatorname{int}N(\eta)$ and $X_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. Its spine is simultaneously $Z=M(P)\cup_S M(K)$ and $Z=(A\cup_{T_0}X_K)\cup_{T_0}S=M(P(K))\cup_{T_0}S$. The product-coordinate deformation to this spine fixes the remaining bottom faces $A$ and $X_K$; the rounded torus collars identify their union with the outgoing boundary. Hence it gives an equivalence of pairs $(E,M(P(K)))\simeq(Z,M(P(K)))$. Excision in these collars identifies its relative homology with $H_*(S,T_0)$. These are actual subspaces and product homotopies, rather than an inference from ordinary homology.

The ordinary generator of $H_1(E;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ defines the specified infinite-cyclic system; the same integral peripheral computation in [F1] shows that it sends $\mu_P$ and $\mu_{P(K)}$ to $t$ and $\mu_K$ to $1$. Its restriction to $S$ is trivial, since the core represents the zero-winding axis. It is also trivial on $M(K)$ and $X_K$: their ordinary first homology is generated by $\mu_K$, so their map to $\mathbb Z$ is zero. Trivial coefficient groups on these pieces are their ordinary $k$ homology tensored with $\Lambda$. This assertion does not require an infinite vector-space splitting: the singular chain complex with trivial coefficients is its $k$ complex tensored with the free $k$ module $\Lambda=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z}kt^n$; cycles, boundaries and exactness commute with this explicit direct sum. In particular $H_1(S;\Lambda)=\Lambda$, $H_1(M(K);\Lambda)=\Lambda[\mu_K]$, and the core inclusion into $M(K)$ is this generator.

Mayer–Vietoris for the first description of $Z$ gives the degree-one difference map $H_1(S;\Lambda)\to H_1(M(P);\Lambda)\oplus H_1(M(K);\Lambda)$ as $a\mapsto([\eta]a,-[\mu_K]a)$. It is injective because its second coordinate is minus the identity of $\Lambda$. The following degree-zero difference map is also injective: it is $\Lambda\to\Lambda/(t-1)\oplus\Lambda$, $a\mapsto(a\bmod(t-1),-a)$. Exactness therefore identifies $H_1(E;\Lambda)$ with the quotient of $H_1(M(P);\Lambda)\oplus\Lambda$ by the displayed graph. The first summand maps isomorphically onto that quotient; explicitly $(x,a)$ maps to $x+[\eta]a$. In particular the core of $S$, equivalently the companion meridian, maps to the image of $[\eta]$ under this isomorphism.

The group $\mathbb Z$ is PTFA, its $k$ group ring is the stated $\Lambda$, and its fraction division ring is $F$. All three boundary components of $E$ have ordinary first Betti number one. The ordinary boundary-cokernel rank is zero by the incoming second-homology generation in [F1]. Applying the full rank comparison in [F2] therefore gives $H_2(E;F)=\operatorname{im}H_2(\partial E;F)$. On $M(P)$ and $M(P(K))$ the restricted infinite-cyclic maps are nontrivial and their first Betti numbers are one, so the other assertion in [F2] gives $H_1(-;F)=0$ there. No vanishing on $M(K)$ is claimed or needed. Consequently [F3] applies to the selected two-component oriented boundary $N=M(P)\sqcup(-M(P(K)))$.

In the pair from step 1.1, the trivial coefficient relative solid-torus calculation gives $H_1(S,T_0;\Lambda)=0$ and $H_2(S,T_0;\Lambda)=\Lambda$, generated by a meridian disk. Indeed $H_1(T_0;\Lambda)\to H_1(S;\Lambda)$ is onto with kernel the meridian summand, and the degree-zero inclusion is an isomorphism. Under the gluing, the meridian boundary of that disk is $\mu_\eta=\lambda_K$. This longitude represents zero in $H_1(X_K;\Lambda)$: the coefficients on $X_K$ are trivial, and the preferred longitude has zero ordinary class in the knot exterior by its zero-linking property, as explicitly computed in [F1]. Its class is therefore zero in $H_1(M(P(K));\Lambda)$. The relative connector $H_2(E,M(P(K));\Lambda)\to H_1(M(P(K));\Lambda)$ is zero on the generator and hence zero. Pair exactness now makes $i_{P(K)}$ an isomorphism, since the following relative group is zero. Together with step 3.1 this proves both asserted isomorphisms and identifies $T[\eta]$ with $[\mu_K]$.

For $x,y\in H_1(M(P);\Lambda)$, the classes $(x,-Tx)$ and $(y,-Ty)$ lie in the kernel of $H_1(N;\Lambda)\to H_1(E;\Lambda)$ by the definition of $T$. The orthogonal sum of the boundary linking forms on this kernel is zero by step 3.2. Reversing the orientation of a closed component negates its cap fundamental class, hence negates inverse-cap duality and the resulting Blanchfield form; its Bockstein and evaluation are unchanged. Bilinearity gives $B_{-M(P(K))}(-Tx,-Ty)=-B_{P(K)}(Tx,Ty)$. Thus kernel isotropy says precisely $B_P(x,y)-B_{P(K)}(Tx,Ty)=0$, proving the claimed isometry. This uses the actual Bockstein linking forms and does not assume any general nonsingularity theorem.

Apply step 5.1 to $x=y=[\eta]$ and use the class identification in step 4.1. It gives $B_{P(K)}([\mu_K],[\mu_K])=B_P([\eta],[\eta])$, so nonzero self-value is preserved. Altering a base path multiplies the based class by some $t^a$; conjugate linearity in the first variable and right linearity in the second multiply its self-value by $t^{-a}$ and $t^a$, whose product is one in the commutative quotient module $F/\Lambda$. All constructions used supplied smooth peripheral products, finite product gluings and the choice-free local homological suppliers. They introduce neither a locally flat annulus-tube assertion nor an unproved arbitrary twisted boundary-generation claim.

derivations.claim: The finite inertia calculations used below require no spectral theorem for an infinite-dimensional space. A nonzero Hermitian form on $\mathbb C^n$ has a vector with nonzero real value: if its diagonal values on the coordinate vectors all vanish, a nonzero off-diagonal entry is detected by a sum $e_i+e_j$ or $e_i+i e_j$. Split off the line of such a vector by subtracting its orthogonal projection, and repeat in the orthogonal complement. Finite induction gives a diagonal form with positive, negative and zero entries. If there are $p$ positive entries, the positive coordinate subspace has dimension $p$, and any subspace of dimension greater than $p$ meets the span of the nonpositive coordinates, so cannot be positive definite. Thus $p$ is the maximal positive dimension; the same argument gives the maximal negative dimension. Congruence preserves these maxima by an invertible change of coordinates, and the diagonal description proves additivity under block sum and sign reversal under negation. For a Hermitian $2\times2$ matrix, its real eigenvalues are $(\operatorname{tr}C\pm\sqrt{(C_{11}-C_{22})^2+4|C_{12}|^2})/2$; their product is its determinant. Hence the trace/determinant tests used below follow explicitly. Every splitting is within a fixed finite-dimensional space.

For integers $b>0$ and $a$, put $w=a-b$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&w\\w&w^2+b\end{pmatrix}$ and $V(a,b)=\begin{pmatrix}A&I_2\\0&B\end{pmatrix}$. Both diagonal blocks are integral and symmetric, so $V(a,b)-V(a,b)^T=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_2\\-I_2&0\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant one. Also $B$ is positive definite: its real quadratic form is $(x+wy)^2+b y^2$, and the same expression with absolute squares works over $\mathbb C$. Its determinant is $b$ and its trace is positive. All these assertions follow directly from the displayed matrices.

For $0<\theta\le\pi$ write $c=1-e^{i\theta}$ and $h=2-2\cos\theta>0$, so $|c|^2=h$. The Hermitian matrix of $V(a,b)$ is $\begin{pmatrix}hA&cI_2\\\bar cI_2&hB\end{pmatrix}$. Subtracting the appropriate multiple of the lower block from the upper block, and the conjugate multiple of its column, is an invertible block congruence to $(hA-B^{-1})\oplus hB$. Its second block contributes signature two. Put $C=hA-B^{-1}$. Since $\operatorname{tr}A=0$ and $B^{-1}$ is positive definite, $\operatorname{tr}C=-\operatorname{tr}B^{-1}<0$. Direct determinant expansion, using $\operatorname{tr}(BA)=2w$ and $\det(BA)=-b$, gives $$\det C=b^{-1}\det(hBA-I_2)=b^{-1}(1-2wh-bh^2).$$ The polynomial has exactly one positive root $$s(a,b)=\frac{-w+\sqrt{w^2+b}}b.$$ For $0<h<s(a,b)$ its determinant is positive and its trace negative, so its two real eigenvalues are negative. At $h=s(a,b)$ it has one negative and one zero eigenvalue. For $h>s(a,b)$ its determinant is negative, so it has one positive and one negative eigenvalue. The signature of $H_\theta(V(a,b))$ is consequently $0,1,2$ in those three cases, respectively. At $\theta=0$ the Hermitian matrix is zero and its signature is zero.

The positive thresholds $s(a,b)$ are dense in $(0,4)$. Indeed fix $r\in(-1,1)$ and set $a_b=\lfloor br\rfloor$ for positive integers $b$. For all sufficiently large $b$, $a_b/b<1$; put $d_b=1-a_b/b>0$. Then $$s(a_b,b)=d_b+\sqrt{d_b^2+1/b},\qquad |s(a_b,b)-2(1-r)|\le2/b+1/\sqrt b.$$ Here $|a_b/b-r|\le1/b$ and $0\le\sqrt{d_b^2+1/b}-d_b\le1/\sqrt b$, which prove the bound. For any desired positive tolerance a sufficiently large integer makes its right side smaller than that tolerance. Given any target in $(0,4)$, take $r$ to be one minus half the target; the explicit floor formula then supplies thresholds arbitrarily close to it. This is a sequence defined by a formula, without selecting any infinite family of witnesses.

The function $h(\theta)=2-2\cos\theta$ is continuous and strictly increasing from $0$ to $4$ on $[0,\pi]$: its derivative is $2\sin\theta>0$ in the interior. Choose two real angles $\alpha<\theta_0<\beta$ in $I$ and small disjoint open intervals around them whose closures are contained respectively in $I\cap(0,\theta_0)$ and $I\cap(\theta_0,\pi)$. Their $h$ images are nonempty intervals in $(0,4)$. Step 3.1 supplies a pair $(a_-,b_-)$ with threshold in the first image and a pair $(a_+,b_+)$ with threshold in the second. If desired these finite witnesses can be specified by enumerating integer pairs by increasing $|a|+b$ and then increasing $a$ and taking the first pair whose explicit threshold is in the relevant interval. Thus the corresponding unique crossing angles satisfy $\theta_-<\theta_0<\theta_+$ and lie in $I$.

Define $V=V(a_-,b_-)\oplus(-V(a_+,b_+))$. Each skew block has determinant one, also after negation, so $\det(V-V^T)=1$. Its Hermitian signature is the difference of the two signatures in step 2.1. Since the thresholds are ordered, it is zero below $\theta_-$, one at $\theta_-$, two on $(\theta_-,\theta_+)$, one at $\theta_+$ and zero above $\theta_+$. It is also zero at zero. This proves all claims on $[0,\pi]$, including nonzero value at $\theta_0$ and vanishing off $I$. Finally $V$ is real, so $H_{-\theta}(V)=\overline{H_\theta(V)}$; conjugation preserves the real eigenvalues and their multiplicities, proving symmetry. The only constructions were finite matrices, explicit integer formulas and two individual integer witnesses. Thus no choice or realization theorem has been used.

derivations.claim: We first describe the finite linking calculation used in the construction. For disjoint oriented polygonal circles with a specified regular plane projection, the linking number is half the signed mixed-crossing sum. This can be proved with finite chains as follows. For the second curve $D$, extend each projected edge vertically downward from its actual height to a plane lying below both curves, and fill its resulting planar projected cycle by the finitely many oriented cone triangles from a plane point. The resulting finite two-chain has boundary $D$. Its intersections with the first curve $C$ occur exactly at the mixed crossings where $C$ is below $D$, with the usual oriented crossing signs. It therefore computes linking as the sum of that subset of signs. The full mixed sum is twice this sum: the difference between the sums where $C$ is below and above $D$ is the algebraic plane intersection of the two projected cycles, which is zero. To check the latter directly, fill one projected cycle by its finite planar cone chain and intersect the other with that chain; the signed endpoints of the resulting finite one-chain cancel. Independence of a finite spanning chain is equally finite: the difference of two such chains is a two-cycle in $\mathbb R^3$, bounded by its cone three-chain. Intersecting that three-chain with the closed curve gives a finite one-chain whose signed boundary sum is zero, so the two intersection numbers agree. Finite subdivisions and perturbations needed to avoid vertices or nontransverse affine intersections avoid only finitely many bad affine conditions; a rational point outside their union exists, for example by trying rational points in a fixed enumeration. Thus no transversality selection on an infinite family is involved. The same computation applies after small local smoothing or to parallel pushed curves, because these changes take place in disjoint boxes without introducing intersections between the two curves.

If $g=0$, use an oriented disk. Otherwise start with an oriented disk and $2g$ labeled orientable rectangular bands. In the cyclic order of their attachment intervals on the disk, put the endpoints of each pair of bands $(2j-1,2j)$ in the alternating order $2j-1,2j,2j-1,2j$, and put the pairs in disjoint successive sectors. Attaching the first band of a pair splits the current boundary into two components; attaching the second joins those two, as direct traversal of the four alternating attachment intervals shows. Each pair therefore preserves one boundary component and raises genus by one. The finite relative cell calculation for the disk and bands has one degree-one generator per band and no relative degree-two cells: collapse the disk, and collapse each band across its width. The relative degree-one boundary is zero because both band ends lie in the connected disk. The pair sequence, with the disk contractible and the degree-zero inclusion an isomorphism, therefore identifies $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^{2g}$. The band cores completed by disk arcs map to its coordinate basis. Choose the disk arcs so that only paired arcs meet, once in their sector. The embedded bands can be routed through a finite regular ribbon diagram: give each band a private twist box and, for every unordered pair, give those two bands one private common box with two parallel strands. Connect these finitely many specified visits by polygonal plane arcs, avoiding the finite existing vertices and arranging transverse double crossings without triple crossings by finitely many rational perturbations. At every other diagram crossing assign one strand above the other, then lift it in a small crossing box. Distinct crossing boxes are disjoint; sufficiently narrow ribbons following these finitely many arcs, and the specified orientable attachments, give an embedded disk-band surface. Arbitrary incidental diagram crossings merely determine its initial matrix and cause no restriction.

Let $W_0$ be the positive-push matrix of this initial surface, computed by step 1.1. Its skew part has zero entries for core pairs whose disk arcs are disjoint. Indeed the annulus sweeping a core from its negative to its positive push misses the other core in that case. In the explicit normal ribbons, sliding both members of the pair $(a_i^-,a_j)$ a small equal distance in the positive normal direction identifies its linking with that of $(a_i,a_j^+)$: their normal heights stay distinct throughout, including over a disk crossing. Linking is symmetric by step 1.1, so the signed-intersection calculation gives equality of the two ordered entries. For a paired pair the sweep meets the other core once in the disk, with sign $+1$ or $-1$, so the difference of its two ordered entries is that sign. In local disk coordinates the sweep is the product of the core arc with a normal interval; its single transverse intersection has multiplicity one. Orient the second core of each pair so that this difference is $+1$. Thus $W_0-W_0^T$ is exactly the displayed standard skew matrix. This calculation is entirely within the given disk and finite ribbon chart; it does not assume a surface-classification or duality theorem. Consequently $W-W_0$ is symmetric.

$$\partial E=M(P)\sqcup M(K)\sqcup(-M(P(K))).$$
For any commutative unital coefficient ring $R$, it has $H_1(E;R)=R$ and $H_2(E;R)=R^2$. The two first boundary components induce the displayed basis in degree two. If $s_L=\alpha_L\cap[M(L)]$ where $\alpha_L\in H^1(M(L);R)$ evaluates as $1$ on the positive meridian, then, in those coordinates,
$$i_*s_{P(K)}=i_*s_P+w\,i_*s_K.$$
In degree one the meridians of $P$, $K$ and $P(K)$ map to $1,w,1$, respectively.

Likewise, for any finite nonempty list of knots $K_1,\ldots,K_q$ with the same supplied peripheral data, there is a compact oriented smooth cobordism $C$ from $\bigsqcup_j M(K_j)$ to $M(K_1\#\cdots\#K_q)$, with $H_1(C;R)=R$ and $H_2(C;R)=R^q$. The incoming degree-two classes are its coordinate basis and the outgoing class maps to their sum. In particular, for $X=E$ or $C$, the outgoing inclusions are injective on $H_1,H_2$ and the union of incoming components surjects onto $H_2(X;R)$.

The peripheral and framing data are supplied, rather than selected by an existence theorem. Their subsequent construction and the homology assertions use no additional choice principle. This is an ordinary-coefficient assertion; arbitrary twisted-coefficient boundary generation is not asserted.

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The proof is choice-free and requires no CW, separation, local path-connectivity or local simple-connectivity assumption.

derivations.claim: Fix $k<n$ and work first in $G=G_{k+1}$. For $k+1\le j<n$, the piece $E_j$ is already present in $W_{k+1}$. Let $A_j$ be the image of the group of its pattern boundary $M(P_j(U))$ in $G$. Its meridian is the image of $\mu_{j+1}$ by [F4], so [F2] implies $A_j\subseteq\langle\!\langle\mu_{j+1}\rangle\!\rangle_G$. By [F4] and [F5], its axis lies in the commutator subgroup of that pattern-boundary group. Its image is $\mu_j$ by [F1]. Hence $$\mu_j\in[A_j,A_j]\subseteq[\langle\!\langle\mu_{j+1}\rangle\!\rangle_G,\langle\!\langle\mu_{j+1}\rangle\!\rangle_G].$$ Only this inclusion is needed; no equality between a single axis normal closure and an entire commutator subgroup is asserted.

Starting with $\mu_n\in G^{(0)}$, descend through the finite range $j=n-1,\ldots,k+1$. If $\mu_{j+1}\in G^{(n-j-1)}$, its normal closure is contained in that derived subgroup because derived subgroups are normal: conjugation preserves every finite commutator word. Step 1.1 then gives $\mu_j\in G^{(n-j)}$. Consequently $\mu_{k+1}\in G^{(n-k-1)}$; when $k=n-1$ this just says $\mu_n\in G$. The companion exterior $X_{J_k}$ is an actual subspace of the outgoing boundary $M(J_{k+1})$. By normal generation of that surgery group in [F2], the entire image of its group, and hence the image of the companion-exterior group, lies in $\langle\!\langle\mu_{k+1}\rangle\!\rangle_G\subseteq G^{(n-k-1)}$. Its longitude lies in its second derived subgroup by [F2]. Expanding the finite commutator products under the inclusion homomorphism therefore puts the longitude image $\lambda_k$ in $G^{(n-k+1)}$.

By [F1], the actual inclusion gives $G_k=G/\langle\!\langle\lambda_k\rangle\!\rangle_G$. Derived subgroups are normal, so step 2.1 puts the entire kernel in $G^{(n-k+1)}$. Apply [F3] with $r=n-k+1$ to obtain exactly the ordinary and mixed-quotient isomorphisms in the Statement, for the actual inclusion map and every supplied finite ring prefix. The image of $\mu_{k+1}$ has depth at least $n-k-1$ by step 2.1, because a homomorphism sends each finite commutator word to the corresponding word of its images. Thus $\mu_k\in G_k^{(n-k)}$.

The topological adjunctions used only supplied three-dimensional boundary collars and the explicit smooth product pieces. Every commutator, representative and path used above belongs to a fixed finite calculation, and [F3] proves the kernel comparisons without an infinite representative selection. Thus the full stated finite-tower naturality and depth assertions hold in the supplied TOP/smooth scope without a choice axiom.

derivations.claim: The supplied contractible basis consists of path-connected open sets, so connectedness implies path-connectedness: path components are open and their complements are open. Form the set of paths $\gamma:o\to x$, identifying two with the same endpoint when the loop $\gamma*(\gamma')^{-1}$ belongs to $N$. The subgroup laws make this an equivalence relation. For a member $U$ of the supplied contractible basis and a path $\gamma$ ending in $U$, let $U_{[\gamma]}$ consist of $[\gamma*\eta]$ for paths $\eta$ lying in $U$ and starting at that endpoint. The projection to $U$ is bijective because any two such paths with the same endpoint are homotopic rel endpoints in $U$. If two such sets over $U$ meet they coincide; for two different basis neighborhoods, a smaller basis neighborhood of a common endpoint shows their intersections contain a basic set of this same form. They therefore define a topology for which $p^{-1}(U)$ is a disjoint union of open sets each homeomorphic to $U$. Surjectivity uses a path to each individual endpoint, rather than selecting all such paths. Thus this is an actual covering space constructed without a representative section.

For completeness the degree-one constant-coefficient calculation needs no universal-coefficient theorem. For any path-connected based space $Y$, concatenate paths by the first-loop-first rule. A constant edge is the boundary of a constant triangle; a path homotopy gives the boundary of its two-triangle prism up to constant endpoint edges; and $uv$ is homologous to $u+v$ by mapping a triangle to the concatenated path with vertex parameters $0,1/2,1$. A reversed path is homologous to the negative path, since its concatenation with the original contracts by retracing. These finite relations show that $[u]_{\mathrm{ab}}\otimes c\mapsto c[u]\in H_1(Y;k)$ is a well-defined additive balanced map $S:\pi_1(Y)_{\mathrm{ab}}\otimes_{\mathbb Z}k\to H_1(Y;k)$. For a fixed finite cycle $z=\sum_e c_e e$, choose paths $\gamma_v$ from the basepoint to the finitely many endpoint images and put $$T_\gamma(z)=\sum_e [\gamma_{e(0)}*e*\gamma_{e(1)}^{-1}]_{\mathrm{ab}}\otimes c_e.$$ Finite choice follows by finite induction in ZF, so these paths exist without an axiom of choice.

A path $\gamma$ lifts from the constant-path point by $t\mapsto[\gamma|_{[0,t]}]$, with the restricted path reparametrized and held stationary after its endpoint. This is continuous on the basic sets of step 1.1, and reaches $[\gamma]$, so $W_N$ is path-connected. For any fixed starting lift, path lifting exists uniquely by finite subdivision into evenly covered basis neighborhoods. A homotopy lifts uniquely by the same finite-grid construction on its compact square: choose a finite fine grid subordinate to the inverse-image cover and extend sheet by sheet, with uniqueness on overlaps. The square is compact metric, so this finite construction uses no choice principle. Hence $p_*$ is injective on fundamental groups, and its image consists exactly of based loops whose lifted endpoint is the constant-path point, that is, exactly $N$. This identifies $\pi_1(W_N)$ with $N$ by the actual projection. The same lifting statement for a singular simplex follows directly by sending a point to the lift obtained along the straight segment from its first vertex; segments joined by a triangle are homotopic inside the simplex, so this gives the unique continuous lift with prescribed first vertex.

Another finite path family changes each loop term by $d_{e(0)}-d_{e(1)}$ in the abelianization. After tensoring, its total coefficient at a vertex is that of the cycle boundary, hence zero. Thus $T_\gamma(z)$ has one uniquely defined value $T(z)$, independent of paths or enlargement of the finite endpoint list. On a singular triangle the loops for edges $01,12,02$ satisfy $L_{01}L_{12}=L_{02}$ because the triangle fills their concatenation, so $T$ kills its signed boundary. For any finite two-chain use the finite union of its vertex images to get the same conclusion termwise, with its $k$ coefficients. Thus $T$ descends to homology. The relations in step 1.2 say $\gamma_{e(0)}*e*\gamma_{e(1)}^{-1}$ is homologous to $\gamma_{e(0)}+e-\gamma_{e(1)}$; in the weighted sum the extra path terms cancel by the cycle condition. Hence $ST=\mathrm{id}$. On a based loop use the constant connector at its endpoint, giving $TS=\mathrm{id}$ on every generator $[u]_{\mathrm{ab}}\otimes c$. This proves the natural isomorphism $H_1(Y;k)\cong\pi_1(Y)_{\mathrm{ab}}\otimes k$. Naturality follows by mapping a finite connector family forward; independence then removes that family from the map. No paths to all points of $Y$ and no basis of an infinite vector space were chosen.

For $g\in G$ and any representative loop $a$, define the right action by $[\gamma]\cdot g=[a^{-1}*\gamma]$. Replacing $a$ by another representative gives the same path class, since $N$ is normal; replacing $\gamma$ by an equivalent path also does. The action law follows from $b^{-1}*a^{-1}=(a*b)^{-1}$, and its maps carry the basic sets in step 1.1 to basic sets. On each fiber it is free and transitive: for paths $\gamma,\delta$ to the same endpoint take the quotient class of $\gamma*\delta^{-1}$, which sends $[\gamma]$ to $[\delta]$. The formula specifies the action uniquely without choosing representatives for all quotient elements. Free $k$-linearization of each fiber gives $\mathcal R_x$; path transport commutes with this right action because it appends a path at the end, while deck action prepends $a^{-1}$. Thus it is a right-$k[G]$ local system, each fiber individually having a torsor point as a free basis. At the basepoint the constant-path point is a specified basis, and transport along $a$ sends it to $[a]=[1]\cdot g^{-1}$, giving exactly the stated inverse convention and a right-linear map.

A basis generator in the local chain group consists of a base singular simplex $\sigma$ together with one point of the covering fiber over its first vertex and a scalar in $k$. Send it to the unique lift of $\sigma$ with that first vertex, given in step 2.1, with the same scalar. Pairs of this kind are in bijection with covering singular simplices: projection gives the inverse map. Both directions are uniquely specified on generators, hence define inverse maps on all finite chains without selecting a lift for each base simplex. For the face omitting the first vertex, the first point of the lifted face is the transport of the old first point along that edge, exactly the local coefficient boundary rule. The other faces keep the first point. Thus the bijection commutes with all signed boundary terms. It commutes with the right deck action on generators too, so gives the claimed actual chain isomorphism of right $k[G]$-module complexes.

Apply steps 1.2 and 2.2 to $Y=W_N$ and combine with steps 2.1 and 4.1. A based loop $u\in N$ lifts to the based loop whose projection is $u$, so its coefficient-one class maps precisely to $[u]\otimes1$. For the right action, move the constant-path base lift by $g=[a]$. The lift of $a^{-1}$ joins the old base lift to that new one. Rebase the translated lift of $u$ by this path and its inverse; its projection is $a^{-1}ua$. Connector contributions cancel in first homology by step 1.2, so this gives the stated conjugation action on $N_{\mathrm{ab}}\otimes k$. Different representatives of $g$ change it by an inner automorphism of $N$, trivial on $N_{\mathrm{ab}}$. The zero criterion is now exactly the displayed isomorphism and its coefficient-one formula; for $N=P^s\pi$ this is the defining next mixed-series kernel. For a based continuous map $f$ carrying $N$ into $N\prime$, the covering map is explicitly $[\gamma]\mapsto[f\circ\gamma]$; the equivalence relation makes it well-defined. It commutes with endpoint projection, the induced quotient-group action and simplex lifting, so step 4.1 is natural for its coefficient maps. Steps 1.2 and 2.2 already prove naturality of the constant-coefficient identification, yielding the stated commutative homology comparison. All covering, chain and homology maps were explicit quotient maps or uniquely defined finite-lift maps, so the full coefficient and choice scope in the Statement is proved.

citations.quote: Every compact Hausdorff topological manifold $M$, with boundary allowed, admits an embedding $e:M\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^N$, an open neighborhood $U$ of $e(M)$ and a retraction $r:U\to e(M)$. Moreover there is a finite Euclidean cubical complex $L$ with $e(M)\subseteq L\subseteq U$, so that $r|_L$ makes $M$ an actual retract of a finite CW complex. No choice principle, smooth or PL structure, triangulation of $M$, or general locally contractible-space retraction theorem is assumed.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Let $W$ be a connected Hausdorff space with a supplied basis of contractible open neighborhoods, $o\in W$, $\pi=\pi_1(W,o)$, and $N\triangleleft\pi$. Put $G=\pi/N$ and let $k$ be any commutative unital ring. Use first-loop-first concatenation in $\pi$. There is a canonical based normal path-class cover $p:W_N\to W$ with $\pi_1(W_N)=N$, whose right deck action is
$$[\gamma]\cdot g=[a^{-1}*\gamma]\quad\text{when }a\in\pi\text{ represents }g.$$
Let $\mathcal R_x$ be the free $k$-module on $p^{-1}(x)$, with its induced right $k[G]$ action and transport along lifted paths. Each fiber is free of rank one as a right $k[G]$-module. Its base fiber is identified with $k[G]$ by the constant-path lift. Thus transport around a based loop $a$ is left multiplication by its quotient image $g^{-1}$.

For this specified right local system, the actual singular chain complex is naturally isomorphic to $C_*(W_N;k)$ as a complex of right $k[G]$-modules, and there is a natural isomorphism
$$H_1(W;\mathcal R)\cong (N/[N,N])\otimes_{\mathbb Z}k.$$
The right action on the last group is $[u]\otimes c\mapsto[a^{-1}ua]\otimes c$ for $g=[a]\in G$. A based loop $u\in N$ with coefficient $1$ corresponds to $[u]\otimes1$. In particular it represents zero in $H_1(W;\mathcal R)$ exactly when it lies in the kernel of $N\to(N/[N,N])\otimes_{\mathbb Z}k$. Taking $N=P^s\pi$ gives exactly the next mixed-series kernel $P^{s+1}\pi$ with coefficient ring $k$. For a based continuous map carrying $N$ into a normal subgroup $N\prime$ of the target fundamental group, these identifications commute with its induced homology maps and quotient-group coefficient maps. This includes every connected Hausdorff manifold, with boundary allowed, and every connected finite polyhedron. No finite CW structure, compactness, finite generation of $\pi$, or choice principle is assumed.

derivations.claim: Use [F1] and retain the component of $L$ containing connected $i(M)$; it is still finite and still retracts onto $M$. Triangulate the finite polyhedron by its given finite geometric structure, choose a spanning tree of its finite one-skeleton, and take one generator for each oriented edge outside the tree. Each two-simplex gives its finite boundary-word relation. These give a finite presentation of $\pi_1(L,i(o))$. Here is the finite van Kampen verification: a tree contracts by successively deleting leaf edges, so the one-skeleton has the free group on the edges outside it. Attaching a two-cell adds the normal relation given by its boundary, by [F2] applied to the cell with a thin based connector strip; the overlap retracts to its boundary circle, and the cell side contracts. Attaching a cell of dimension at least three adds no relation or generator because the same overlap is its simply connected boundary sphere. A sphere of dimension at least two is simply connected by [F2] on its two punctured-coordinate charts: they are Euclidean spaces and contract, and their overlap is path-connected. This verifies the presentation through the finite list of cells. A path from $i(o)$ to a chosen tree vertex changes basepoint and only conjugates these finitely many loops.

Put $P=\pi_1(L,i(o))=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_a\mid r_1,\ldots,r_b\rangle$. The based endomorphism $e=i_*r_*$ is idempotent and has image $i_*\pi_1(M,o)$, with $i_*$ injective because $r_*i_*=\mathrm{id}$. Choose a finite word $w_j$ representing $e(x_j)$ for each of the finitely many generators. Consider $$Q=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_a\mid r_1,\ldots,r_b,\ x_1w_1^{-1},\ldots,x_aw_a^{-1}\rangle.$$ The map $e:P\to\operatorname{im}e$ kills these additional relations because $e^2=e$, so descends to $Q$. Conversely include $\operatorname{im}e$ in $P$ and pass to $Q$. This gives inverse maps: on $e(x_j)$ the first composite is $e^2(x_j)=e(x_j)$; on the generating $x_j$ of $Q$ the second is $w_j=x_j$ by its new relation. Hence $Q\cong\operatorname{im}e\cong\pi_1(M,o)$, proving finite presentability by an explicit finite quotient, rather than assuming retracts preserve finite presentation.

Realize the finite presentation $Q$ by a bouquet of its generator circles and one two-cell per relator; the same [F2] calculation gives fundamental group $Q$. Map each generator circle to its based loop in $M$ under the isomorphism in step 2.1. Each relator has trivial based class, so has a based nullhomotopy; choose one for each of the finitely many relators and extend over its two-cell. This gives a based map inducing exactly that isomorphism. For each specified $\gamma_h$, choose one finite word $v_h$ in these generators representing its based class, add a new generator $y_h$ and the relation $y_hv_h^{-1}$, and map $y_h$ exactly by $\gamma_h$. A nullhomotopy of its relation extends this map. The added generator can be eliminated from the presentation, so the induced fundamental-group map is still the same isomorphism. This particular presentation complex has a finite polyhedral model. Triangulate every generator circle by three edges and read each nonempty relator on a subdivided boundary circle, so each boundary edge maps homeomorphically to one graph edge. Insert its mapping cylinder before attaching the disk. Each cylinder rectangle has distinct bottom endpoints in the graph and distinct private top endpoints; triangulate it by a fresh center and its four boundary edges. The private center distinguishes different rectangles even when their bottom edges coincide, and neighboring vertical sides agree, so these are finitely many honest simplices. Cone each top circle to a fresh vertex to attach its disk. The cylinder plus disk is just a disk with an extra annular collar, so this changes no underlying presentation space or graph marking. Empty relators may be omitted without affecting the group; with no generators the point suffices until marked generators are added. Thus $K$ has a finite simplicial triangulation of its underlying space, and its contractible open-star basis, while retaining its original one-vertex CW description. These operations produce the asserted finite two-complex with its actual marked loops.

The normal subgroup pulled back along this isomorphism maps isomorphically onto $N$. Apply the explicit normal path-class construction and finite-cycle comparison of [F3] to the map in step 3.1; the finite triangulation in step 3.1 supplies its required contractible-neighborhood basis. Its chain-map naturality identifies the actual map on local $H_1$ with the isomorphism of the covering subgroups' abelianizations tensored with $k$, which is an isomorphism with its explicitly induced inverse. Only the finite polyhedron, its group presentation, individual words and finitely many nullhomotopies were selected. No homotopy equivalence between $M$ and $K$ or finite CW type of $M$ was inferred. This proves precisely the stated choice-free presentation and degree-one comparison.

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair and $\mathcal L$ a left $R$-module local system on $X$. The cellular local chain complex computes singular local homology:
$$H_n\bigl(C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H_n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$
The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms. Intrinsically,
$$C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\cong H_n(X^n\cup A,X^{n-1}\cup A;\mathcal L).$$

derivations.claim: Apply [F1], and pull the given coefficient system to $K$. The induced fundamental-group map is an isomorphism and matches $\mu$, so [F2] identifies the actual $H_1$ of $K$ with that of $M$ for $\Lambda$ and every $k[t,t^{-1}]$. Use [F3] on this actual finite two-complex. Its chain groups are finite free, with $C_0=\Lambda$, a basis of one-cells including $e_\mu$, and a finite basis of two-cells. Cell lifts and orientations require only finitely many choices. Their incidence coefficients reduce under every constant-ring map, so coefficient change on these finite cellular chains is literally coefficientwise change in their Laurent matrices. In particular augmentation $t=1$ gives exactly the ordinary integral cellular complex of $K$.

If the other oriented one-cells have images $n_j\in\mathbb Z$, their degree-one boundaries are $t^{-n_j}-1$, while $d_1e_\mu=t^{-1}-1$. Set $z=-t e_\mu$, so $d_1z=t-1$. Write $q_j=(t^{-n_j}-1)/(t-1)\in\Lambda$, an explicit finite geometric sum also for negative exponents, and replace $e_j$ by $f_j=e_j-zq_j$. This is an invertible triangular basis change with $C_1=\Lambda z\oplus\Lambda^r\langle f_j\rangle$ and $d_1f_j=0$. Multiplication by $t-1$ is injective in $k[t,t^{-1}]$ for every commutative $k$: the top nonzero coefficient of a nonzero finite Laurent list remains a nonzero top coefficient after multiplication by this monic polynomial. Thus $\ker d_1$ is exactly the $f_j$ summand, both integrally and after every constant-ring change. Since $d_1d_2=0$, the $z$ row of $d_2$ is zero. Let $A(t)$ be its remaining $r\times s$ matrix, giving $H_1(K;\Lambda)=\operatorname{coker}A(t)$ and $H_1(K;k[t,t^{-1}])=\operatorname{coker}A_k(t)$.

At $t=1$, $d_1=0$ and the integral first homology is therefore $\mathbb Z[z]\oplus\operatorname{coker}A(1)$. The marked class $z$ maps to $-[\mu]$, a free generator of $H_1(M;\mathbb Z)$ by hypothesis and [F1]–[F2]. Hence $\operatorname{coker}A(1)=0$ and $A(1):\mathbb Z^s\to\mathbb Z^r$ is onto. For each of the finitely many coordinate vectors choose one preimage, giving an integer $s\times r$ matrix $S$ with $A(1)S=I_r$. Put $D(t)=A(t)S$ and $\Delta_0(t)=\det D(t)$. Then $\Delta_0(1)=1$. The adjugate identity $D\,\operatorname{adj}D=\Delta_0 I_r$, proved by finite signed minor expansion, gives $\Delta_0\Lambda^r\subseteq\operatorname{im}D\subseteq\operatorname{im}A$. Thus $\Delta_0$ annihilates the presented first homology. The same identity is an identity of integer Laurent matrices, so holds after every coefficient change as well. For $r=0$, use the empty determinant one; the corresponding first homology is zero.

Normalize $\Delta_0$ by a power of $t$ so its smallest exponent is zero, obtaining the asserted polynomial $\Delta$ with nonzero constant term. This multiplies it by a Laurent unit and retains $\Delta(1)=1$ and every annihilation assertion. Via the natural identifications in steps 1.1–2.1 this is the actual coefficient map on local $H_1$, not just an abstract isomorphism of modules. All selections in step 3.1 were finite preimages of a finite standard basis, and the remaining operations were finite integer or Laurent-matrix calculations. This proves the full scope without a choice axiom or a finite CW claim about $M$.
