citations.quote:
Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff manifold, with boundary allowed, with a specified based loop $\mu$ whose integral homology class freely generates $H_1(M;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. Let $\phi:\pi_1(M)\to\mathbb Z$ be the abelianization taking $\mu$ to $1$, put $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$, and use its associated normal-cover right coefficient system, whose transport around a loop $a$ is left multiplication by $t^{-\phi(a)}$ in the based fiber.

There is a finite Laurent matrix $A(t)$ such that
$$H_1(M;\Lambda)\cong\operatorname{coker}A(t),$$
naturally on changing the constant coefficient ring from $\mathbb Z$ to any commutative unital ring $k$. More precisely the actual coefficient map gives
$$H_1(M;\Lambda)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}k\cong H_1(M;k[t,t^{-1}]).$$
There is a polynomial $\Delta(t)\in\mathbb Z[t]$ with $\Delta(0)\ne0$ and $\Delta(1)=1$ annihilating $H_1(M;\Lambda)$; its coefficient image annihilates $H_1(M;k[t,t^{-1}])$ for every $k$. In particular $\Delta$ is primitive and its reduction modulo any prime is nonzero. No choice principle, finite CW type, triangulation, smoothness or Seifert presentation for $M$ is assumed.

Put $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$ and $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q[t,t^{-1}]$. Let $\Delta\in\Lambda$ be nonzero and primitive, meaning that the greatest common divisor of its finitely many integer coefficients is one. Define
$$T_\Delta=\{x\in\mathbb Q(t)/\Lambda:\Delta x=0\}.$$
The natural map $\mathbb Q(t)/\Lambda\to\mathbb Q(t)/\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}$ is injective on $T_\Delta$.

For a prime $p$ such that $\bar\Delta\ne0$ in $\Lambda_p=\mathbb F_p[t,t^{-1}]$, there is a well-defined additive reduction map
$$\rho_{p,\Delta}:T_\Delta\longrightarrow\mathbb F_p(t)/\Lambda_p,\qquad [a/\Delta]\longmapsto[\bar a/\bar\Delta],\quad a\in\Lambda.$$
It satisfies $\rho_{p,\Delta}(b x)=\bar b\,\rho_{p,\Delta}(x)$ for $b\in\Lambda$. For every nonzero $x\in T_\Delta$, one can compute a nonzero integer $D$ from $\Delta$ and a chosen representative $a/\Delta$ such that $\rho_{p,\Delta}(x)\ne0$ for every prime $p\nmid D$. No choice principle or factorization theorem for arbitrary rings is assumed. This is a map on the specified annihilated quotient module; no global reduction homomorphism from $\mathbb Q(t)$ to $\mathbb F_p(t)$ is asserted.

Let $R$ be a unital ring with $1\ne0$ and no zero divisors. Suppose both Ore conditions hold: any two nonzero elements have a nonzero common right multiple and a nonzero common left multiple. Let $R\subseteq K$ be a unital embedding into a division ring such that every element of $K$ is a right fraction $as^{-1}$ with $a\in R$ and $0\ne s\in R$.

For every right $R$-module $M$, the right $K$-module $M\otimes_RK$ is represented by fractions $[m,s]$ with $m\in M$ and $0\ne s\in R$, corresponding to $m\otimes s^{-1}$. The equality criterion is
$$[m,s]=[n,t]\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{there exist }0\ne u,v\in R\text{ with }su=tv\text{ and }mu=nv.$$
In particular, $[m,s]=0$ if and only if $ma=0$ for some $0\ne a\in R$. Thus the kernel of $M\to M\otimes_RK$, $m\mapsto m\otimes1$, is exactly the set of elements with a nonzero right annihilator, and $M\otimes_RK=0$ if and only if every element of $M$ has a nonzero right annihilator.

The functor $-\otimes_RK$ is exact on arbitrary right $R$-modules, so $K$ is flat as a left $R$-module. For every chain complex $C_\bullet$ of right $R$-modules, the canonical map gives a natural isomorphism
$$H_i(C_\bullet)\otimes_RK\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }H_i(C_\bullet\otimes_RK)$$
for every integer $i$. No finite-generation, finite-presentation or boundedness assumption on the modules or complexes is required.

The corresponding left-module assertions also hold: $K$ is flat as a right $R$-module, $1\otimes m$ is zero in $K\otimes_RM$ precisely when $am=0$ for some $0\ne a\in R$, and $K\otimes_R-$ commutes with the homology of arbitrary left-module chain complexes. All assertions require no choice axiom.

Let $M$ be a compact oriented boundaryless Hausdorff topological $n$-manifold and let $\mathcal L$ be a local system of abelian groups. Cap with its integral orientation class induces isomorphisms
$$H^p(M;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;\mathcal L)$$
for every integer $p$, without a choice principle. The maps respect any coefficient-ring action commuting with transport, and in particular apply to local systems of modules over a noncommutative ring by forgetting to abelian groups and retaining that action. No smoothness, triangulation or prescribed finite CW structure is assumed.

Let $(M,o)$ be a compact connected based Hausdorff manifold, let $R$ be an involutive unital ring, and supply a rank-one right-$R$ local system $\mathcal R$ with an identification $\mathcal R_o=R$. Assume every based-loop monodromy is left multiplication by a unit $u$ satisfying $\bar u=u^{-1}$. Equip the base fiber with the standard Hermitian form $h_o(a,b)=\bar a b$. Transport extends this to a path-independent parallel Hermitian form $h$ on $\mathcal R$. Put $C_*=C_*(M;\mathcal R)$. For a right $R$-module $P$, write $\overline P$ for its conjugate left module, with $r\cdot\bar p=\overline{p\bar r}$.

The left-$R$ cochain complex $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R)$ is the intrinsic cochain complex of the left-$R$ local system with fiber $R$ and transport $a\mapsto au^{-1}$. Relative to the supplied parallel Hermitian form, that local system is naturally isomorphic to $\overline{\mathcal R}$ by $\bar v\mapsto[w\mapsto h(v,w)]$. The identifications are independent of unitary fiber frames; an arbitrary change of Hermitian structure is not asserted to preserve them. If $M$ is oriented, boundaryless and of dimension $n$, cap duality therefore gives
$$H^p(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R))\cong\overline{H_{n-p}(C_*)}.$$
If $R\subseteq K$ is an embedding into an involutive division ring extending the involution, the same conclusion is valid for $K$, with $C_*\otimes_R K$ in the homology target. If $R$ is involution-stable in $K$, the complex $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,K/R)$ is the corresponding intrinsic left-$R$ cochain complex with fiber $K/R$ and transport by right multiplication by $u^{-1}$. These identifications require no choice principle and commute with the coefficient maps $R\to K\to K/R$.

Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff manifold, $o\in M$, and $R$ a unital ring. One can construct paths $\gamma_x$ from $o$ to every $x\in M$, with $\gamma_o$ constant, by fixed rules from one finite atlas and finitely many connecting paths. Let $\mathcal R$ be a right-$R$ local system with a supplied identification $\mathcal R_o=R$ and transport given by left multiplication by units, with monodromy image $H\le R^\times$. Its twisted singular complex has an explicit chain decomposition $C_*(M;\mathcal R)=C'_*\oplus Q_*$ after a change of free bases, where $C'_0=R$, $C'_* $ is free, and $Q_*$ is contractible with its only nonzero differential an identity from degree one to degree zero. Moreover
$$\operatorname{im}(d'_1)=\sum_{h\in H}(h-1)R.$$
The decomposition and its dual cochain homotopy equivalences require no choice principle. In particular this image is principal if $H$ is cyclic, if it equals $R$, or if every right ideal of $R$ is principal.

Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff manifold with a basepoint, and let $0\to\mathcal A\xrightarrow{i}\mathcal B\xrightarrow{q}\mathcal C\to0$ be a short exact sequence of local systems of abelian groups on $M$. There is a natural coefficient Bockstein making the sequence
$$H^1(M;\mathcal B)\xrightarrow{q_*}H^1(M;\mathcal C)\xrightarrow{\beta}H^2(M;\mathcal A)\xrightarrow{i_*}H^2(M;\mathcal B)$$
exact at its two middle terms. In particular $\beta$ is an isomorphism if $H^1(M;\mathcal B)=H^2(M;\mathcal B)=0$. No choice principle is assumed. If the local systems and maps have a commuting coefficient-ring action, the sequence and Bockstein respect it.

derivations.claim: Choose $\Delta$ from [F1] and put $\delta=\Delta^*=\Delta(t^{-1})$. Both are primitive and evaluate to one at $t=1$. In each field coefficient case their reductions are nonzero. By [F3], localization annihilates the first homology because its annihilator becomes invertible; thus $H_1(M;\mathbb Q(t))=0$ for the integral and rational systems and $H_1(M;\mathbb F_p(t))=0$ for every prime system. The unlocalized first homology is torsion in each case, since the same nonzero annihilator kills it. These are statements about the actual coefficient homology of $M$ by [F1] and arbitrary-chain localization; no finite CW structure is used.

For any of these coefficient inclusions $R\subset K$, the degree-two dual $K$ cohomology is zero by [F4] and $H_1(M;K)=0$. The degree-one dual $K$ cohomology is zero too: use [F5]'s one-vertex chain model with $C_0=K$. Its $d_1$ image is zero or all of $K$. In the first case $H_1=0$ makes every degree-one chain a boundary, so every dual one-cocycle is zero. In the second choose one $v$ with $d_1v=1$; split off $vK$, and use $\ker d_1=\operatorname{im}d_2$ to see that each dual one-cocycle is a coboundary. The natural exact coefficient segment in [F5] therefore makes $\beta:H^1(M;(K/R)^\vee)\to H^2(M;R^\vee)$ an isomorphism. Closed cap duality and evaluation consequently define all the displayed linking forms on the whole first homology. This step does not assert that the final evaluation map is an isomorphism.

Fix $x,y$ and take an integral dual two-cocycle $a$ representing the inverse-cap class of $\bar x$. Since $x\Delta=0$ by [F1] and duality is linear on the conjugate module, $\delta[a]=0$. Thus one whole integral dual one-cochain $c$ satisfies $\partial^*c=\delta a$. The $K$-cochain $b=c/\delta$ satisfies $\partial^*b=a$, so its quotient is a one-cocycle with Bockstein $[a]$. Uniqueness of the inverse in step 2.1 gives $$B_{\mathbb Z}(x,y)=[c(y)/\delta]\in\mathbb Q(t)/\Lambda.$$ In particular this value lies in the $\delta$-annihilated subgroup. This construction uses one integral cochain witness from a zero cohomology class; it neither chooses quotient representatives on all simplices nor asks an infinite product of surjections to be onto.

Use the actual finite-atlas path frames of [F5] simultaneously for the coefficient systems. The integral singular chain group is free on its actual singular simplices and its reduction is the corresponding $\Lambda_p$ chain group, with the same transition monomials reduced coefficientwise. Hence every integral dual cochain has a canonical forward reduction: reduce its value on each basis simplex and extend $\Lambda_p$-linearly. This defines a function without selecting any preimages, and commutes with the cochain differential. Thus $\partial^*c_p=\delta_p a_p$; since $\delta_p\ne0$, $c_p/\delta_p$ is a field-valued primitive of $a_p$. Cap and evaluation are finite simplex formulas, so coefficient change sends $[a]$ to the inverse-cap class of $\overline{x_p}$ and gives $c_p(y_p)=(c(y))_p$. By step 2.1 the actual mod-$p$ pairing therefore equals $[c_p(y_p)/\delta_p]=\rho_{p,\delta}(B_{\mathbb Z}(x,y))$. The same argument over $\mathbb Q$ uses the honest inclusion $\Lambda\to\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}$ and the same fraction $c/\delta$, giving exactly the asserted rational quotient identity. In a chosen unitary frame $e$, the inverse intrinsic-dual identification sends a functional $f$ to $\overline{e\,\overline{f(e)}}$; reducing its coefficient and then taking this expression is the same as reducing that expression, because the involution and all ring operations commute with reduction. Thus the intrinsic-dual/conjugate identifications in [F4] respect these fixed frames as well, so no scalar side or unmarked gauge change occurs.

If the integral self-value is nonzero, it belongs to $T_\delta$ by step 3.1. Apply [F2]. Its rational image is nonzero, and its specified prime reductions are nonzero away from the finite exceptional integer constructed there. The identities in step 4.1 identify these values with the actual rational and prime Blanchfield self-values. Every prime denominator is valid because $\delta_p(1)=1$. Compactness was used in the proved finite-presentation/annihilator and finite-atlas cochain suppliers; all remaining primitive, reduction, cap and evaluation operations were forward maps or individual cochain witnesses. Thus the full integral-to-rational and integral-to-prime nonzero conclusions hold without any added choice, smoothness, CW or global fraction-field reduction assumption.

For every $0<\theta_0<\pi$ and every open interval $I\subset(0,\pi)$ containing $\theta_0$, there is an explicit integral $8\times8$ matrix $V$ with $\det(V-V^T)=1$ such that the finite Hermitian matrix
$$H_\theta(V)=(1-e^{i\theta})V+(1-e^{-i\theta})V^T$$
has signature $2$ at $\theta_0$ and signature zero for all $\theta\in[0,\pi]\setminus I$. Its signature takes only the values $0,1,2$ on $[0,\pi]$ and is invariant under $\theta\mapsto-\theta$. Moreover, its signature equals $2$ throughout an open interval containing $\theta_0$. No choice principle, classification of Seifert forms, realization by a knot, or infinite-dimensional spectral theorem is assumed.

Let $g\ge0$ and let $W$ be an integral $2g\times2g$ matrix satisfying
$$W-W^T=\bigoplus_{j=1}^g\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
A finite construction produces a compact connected smooth oriented surface $F\subset S^3$ with one boundary component and an ordered basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ such that
$$\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)=W_{ij}.$$
Here $a_i^+$ is a sufficiently small push in the positive oriented normal direction to $F$. The construction uses a finite disk-and-band diagram, finitely many full twists and pairwise clasps, and finite local smoothing. It needs no choice axiom, abstract classification of Seifert forms, generic-projection theorem for arbitrary curves, or normal-neighborhood theorem for locally flat surfaces in four dimensions.

derivations.claim: Let $\Theta$ be the finite set $\{0,\pi\}\cup\{2\pi r/p_j:1\le j\le m,\ 1\le r\le(p_j-1)/2\}$. All displayed interior angles are distinct except when both indices and residues agree: equality $r/p_j=s/p_\ell$ for distinct primes would force $p_j$ to divide $r$ or $p_\ell$, impossible in the stated residue ranges. The target $\theta_i=2\pi/p_i$ is one of these interior angles. Its distance from every other member of $\Theta$ is positive; let $\delta_i$ be one third of the finite minimum of these distances. Thus $I_i=(\theta_i-\delta_i,\theta_i+\delta_i)\subset(0,\pi)$ contains none of the other angles in $\Theta$. Choose the least positive integer $N_i$ with $2N_i>C_i$, which exists by the Archimedean property of the reals. All these are finite operations on the supplied list.

Use [F1] with $\theta_i,I_i$ to obtain the exact matrix $B_i$ there, and let $\widetilde V_i$ be the block sum of $N_i$ copies of $B_i$. Its signature is $N_i$ times that of $B_i$ by finite inertia additivity. In each positive four-dimensional skew block reorder $(e_1,e_2,f_1,f_2)$ as $(e_1,f_1,e_2,f_2)$; in each negative skew block use $(e_1,-f_1,e_2,-f_2)$. Their block sum is an explicit signed permutation $P_i$ for which $V_i=P_i^T\widetilde V_iP_i$ has standard symplectic skew part. Congruence preserves every Hermitian signature by [F1]. Apply [F2] with $g=4N_i$ to realize exactly $V_i$ on an actual smooth one-boundary surface, whose oriented boundary is $K_i$. Thus the constructed knot and chosen matrix have the required nonnegative, conjugate-symmetric signature function, equal to $2N_i$ at $\omega_i$. No mirroring or change of knot orientation is needed to make its sign positive.

At any nonidentity $p_j$-th root, complex conjugation puts its angle in $\Theta\setminus\{0,\pi\}$. If $j\ne i$, that angle is outside $I_i$, so its signature is zero by [F1]. If $j=i$, only the residues $r\equiv\pm1$ give the angle $\theta_i$; every other nonidentity residue gives another angle of $\Theta$ outside $I_i$ and has signature zero. At the identity all Hermitian matrices in the definition are zero, so their signature is zero as well. The two residues $\pm1$ are distinct because $p_i$ is odd. Their values are both $2N_i$, so summing the exact finite list gives the displayed averages, with no integration or analytic identification. These constructions and the matrix-realization choices are finite and explicit; the statement concerns the actual supplied Seifert surfaces. This proves the full finite separation and height assertions.
